#4416. Speeders just got lucky: the new Chevy police Silverado is NOT electric

Say what you will about America’s police forces, but they are loyal – often to each other, and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle. And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.

A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.

If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because Electrek readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV, which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm, along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles – which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence, and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric.

Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about – and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score, so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.

A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear – and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue.

I don’t know why anyone would use a truck as a persuit vehicle? It seems reckless inefficient and ineffective.

Guess we are on the topic of us policing…

#4415. Why Chinese Cars Are Packed With Features Americans Don't Always Ask For

Mercedes Sales Plunge 31% in China as It Eyes Bigger US Push

Car Loan Fraud Is Costing Billions As AI Makes Scams Harder To Spot

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

Why do some Chinese cars come loaded with technology while American vehicles often put affordability first? A recent study offers an interesting explanation.

Nissan Armada Jungle Patrol Ditches Roof and Luxury for Serious Off-Roading

Ferrari Almost Quit Formula 1, And This $1 Million Pace Car Tells the Story

Inside Doug DeMuro's Secret Underground Car Garage

McLaren's Manual V8 McL 6GT Makes Its Public Debut in Las Vegas

What do you first consider when buying a car? Is it the price, the technology included, or perhaps the safety features? It turns out that the answer varies considerably depending on where you live. A recent study by Bain & Company highlights a noticeable difference between the buying priorities of American and Chinese consumers, offering some insight into why vehicles from these two markets can be so different.

Bain’s 2026 Global Auto Consumer Survey polled over 12,000 car shoppers around the globe. The big takeaway? What people care about most when picking out a car isn’t the same everywhere.

For Americans, price is king – 68% say it’s their number one concern. Europeans aren’t far behind at 62%. But in China, it’s a whole different ballgame: 58% of buyers put technology and features at the top of their wish list.

It’s not exactly shocking when you look at the bigger picture. With living costs climbing in the US and Europe, keeping things affordable is a must. Meanwhile, Chinese automakers are locked in a price war, so cars there are cheaper – and that leaves plenty of room to pack in extra tech as a selling point.

These preferences help explain why Chinese automakers have become particularly generous when it comes to technology and equipment. It’s not unusual for vehicles from Chinese brands to come with large infotainment displays, multiple digital interfaces, advanced driver assistance systems, and comfort features that would otherwise be optional extras elsewhere.

In China, where buyers are tech-hungry, automakers are in a full-on features arms race. If it plugs in, lights up, or talks back, it’s probably in there – everything but the kitchen sink.

American automakers, meanwhile, still have to pay close attention to pricing, particularly in the mass-market segment. That doesn’t mean American buyers don’t appreciate technology. In fact, 49% of US respondents still ranked technology and features among their top considerations.

Brand loyalty is another interesting difference. According to Bain, 79% of American mass-market buyers and 72% of premium buyers considered only established brands during their previous purchase. In China, brand loyalty is considerably weaker, with 24% of respondents saying they don’t care about the brand at all.

Regional differences aren’t the only factor shaping the automotive market. Age also plays a considerable role, particularly when it comes to electric vehicles.

Bain’s findings show that younger buyers are generally more receptive to battery electric vehicles (BEVs). Around 50% of Gen Y and Gen Z consumers in the US and China are open to purchasing one. In Europe, the figure reaches 46% for younger buyers.

Older buyers? Not so much. Just 22% of older Americans are willing to go electric, compared to 50% of the younger crowd. China bucks the trend, though – over half of all age groups there are open to EVs.

So, what does this mean? Car companies can’t make the same model for everyone and expect it to work. What excites a young Chinese buyer might not interest an older American. For global brands, understanding these differences is as important as creating new car technology.

#4414. An Uncompromising Fraternal Twin: We Drive the All-Electric 2027 BMW i3

It may not look all that different, but the electric i3 sedan differs from its 3-series siblings in a few key ways.

While BMW’s latest i3 may look like a carbon copy of its gas-powered 3-series sibling, using the gasser to underpin the EV would incur all manner of compromise. BMW did this with its i4 and the 430i models, and the concessions are obvious. In order to get a battery-electric powertrain tucked in the 430i’s body, BMW had to limit the battery size while using air springs to manage the car’s newfound mass. BMW wasn’t willing to make those sacrifices for its electric 3, and as a result, the i3 is actually quite different from its internal-combustion sibling.

The Munich-built BMW i3 50 xDrive sedan shares nothing with the new Dingolfing-made M350 and 330 models, except the front grille, the mirror housings, and possibly the door handles. Everything else is different, and that is reflected by a 1.5-inch stretch in wheelbase, plus some extra height and width. The length, on the other hand, differs only by a few hairs. But the difference is so much more than numbers on a page. Without having to worry about fitting an inline-six under the hood, the i3’s cabin is pushed forward, and the windshield glass picks up some extra rake. The Neue Klasse styling applied to both cars is effective at hiding these differences, but keen eyes may still pick up on the slightly steeper hood and the shorter front-wheel-to-door-edge gap.

See all results for new 2027 BMW i3 for sale near 80537

Adjusting the wheelbase and vehicle height was necessary to fit the electric drivetrain BMW wanted in there, and as a result, we think the i3 50 xDrive outshines the i4. The prime mover is a current-excited synchronous rear motor making 322 horsepower and 321 pound-feet of torque, the same kind of e-motor in the i4. However, the i3’s front motor has been changed to a 165-hp, 188-lb-ft induction motor, and that alteration makes it more efficient because there is less drag when it isn’t engaged. It’s more efficient at speed too. Accounting for the usual fuzzy EV-motor math, the i3 50’s full output is a meaty 463 horses and 476 pound-feet, enough to push the electric 3 to 60 mph in an estimated 4.2 seconds.

Also unlike the i4, the i3’s battery is not a limit in any way, shape, or form. It’s much more capacious, toting 112 kWh instead of the i4’s 84 kWh. We estimate the range at a fantastic 450 miles (the EPA has yet to rate it), which is a bit higher than BMW’s own number, since the electric iX3 SUV’s official range also surpassed BMW’s initial internal figure. The two vehicles share a powertrain, so we figure the powertrain’s overachieving nature will transfer from SUV to sedan too. On the charging front, the pack’s 800-volt architecture means it can gulp down electricity at 400 kilowatts (if you can find a charger that can support it). A NACS port is standard equipment, with an included adapter for SAE Combo charging.

See all results for new 2027 BMW i3 for sale near 80537

Despite leaving the optional M adaptive dampers at home, the car we drove seemed expertly tuned, with a ride that was taut but never too firm. The battery’s low mass helped keep the car feeling planted in corners, with just enough roll stiffness to keep body lean disciplined without introducing harshness or head toss to upset the proceedings.

And we pushed it hard in corners, too. Some of this feeling comes from BMW’s “Heart of Joy” computer, which sorts out the steering, friction braking, regenerative braking, throttle inputs, and more—in a claimed one-tenth of the time that previous BMW software stacks required. Brake-based rear differential action, something we usually don’t care for, was silky smooth in this system and felt for all the world like an electronically controlled rear diff. Brake response is uncommonly good, and there is enough regenerative braking capacity that nearly all your routine stops will be handled magnetically.

The one thing we were less effervescent about was the steering feel. The i3’s helm is certainly accurate and direct enough, but it doesn’t quite have the feel and feedback of the gas-powered M350 we drove (and reviewed separately). Perhaps that differentiator is there intentionally; after all, there’s a sportier i3 M60 model coming.

At least the i3 we drove didn’t have the dorky steering wheel with odd vertical spokes. (The optional M Sport wheel puts said spokes in a vastly more normal location.) BMW’s trick Panoramic Vision screen works even better in the i3 than it does in the M350, because the dash-spanning display strip is more visible above the wheel, yet it doesn’t hide the road. The taller but more steeply angled hood works in its favor, for sure. The central touchscreen is the same 17.9-inch display found in the M350 and has all the same characteristics. On the positive side, it looks great, and the angled shape is quite natural. On the other hand, let’s just say that vent aiming is better done manually, rather than via touchscreen controls, and there are other functions that could benefit from a real button or two. You can save a few bucks by not opting for the head-up display, which seems redundant when you already have a wealth of information at the base of the windscreen.

We also like the i3’s soaring panoramic glass roof, which provides an abundance of headroom. Rear-seat space is slightly larger than the M350’s, but toe space beneath the front seat can be tighter if the front occupant has their chair lowered to the floor. BMW doesn’t have a U.S.-specific figure for trunk space just yet, but preliminary German figures place its 15 cubic feet just one cube in arrears of the M350 gasser.

The BMW i3 50 xDrive will launch in the first quarter of 2027, right alongside the gas-powered 3-series lineup. It starts at $62,850, which seems like a great deal for all you get. The i3 feels mighty special and has the potential to draw new buyers into the electric fold. It’s got gobs of range, it charges fast, and it delivers speed and poise like a proper BMW.

#4413. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4412. Bigger, badder Section 179 tax deduction could POWER UP fleet electrification [update]

With national diesel prices inching towards $7/gallon and Tesla’s $290,000 Semi trucks finally making their way to paying customers, it’s worth revisiting how Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBA) helped beef up the Section 179 deduction, and look again at how it could help your fleet ditch diesel sooner rather than later.

At the core of this thinking is the fact that the IRS does not distinguish between fuel choices, so there’s no separate depreciation category for electric- vs. diesel-fueled commercial trucks. The relevant classifications, then, are the vehicle’s use and property classes, and under the IRS’ depreciation guidelines, tractor units designed for over-the-road use are classified as 3-year properties and fall under the 20-year recovery threshold for 100% bonus depreciation, Tesla’s electric Semi can benefit from 179 just like their diesel-powered competitors. But don’t get me wrong – this isn’t just great news for Tesla Semi buyers. Electric garbage trucks, electric vocational trucks, battery electric reefer trailers, and even some big electric forklifts can potentially benefit from the same accelerated depreciation rules, since the IRS lists these as, “specialized business vehicles,” with no distinction between electric, diesel, natural gas, hydrogen, magic pixie dust, anything else.

There’s been some additional movement on the tax front since our original article, too. Earlier this year, the IRS issued Notice 2026-11, providing additional guidance on the permanent restoration of 100% bonus depreciation for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025. That means that eligible businesses might be able to combine Section 179 expensing with bonus depreciation when ordering qualifying fleet equipment – and ordering is the key word. The IRS has specific rules for determining when equipment is considered acquired under a written, binding contract, and your tax professional and truck dealer can probably help you figure out a way to make those rules work in your favor.

You can check out the original article (with a few corrections sprinkled in to align with the latest guidance from Notice 2026-11 and Publication 946) below. Give it a read, read the disclaimer twice, then let us know what you think in the comments.

After the Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit (Section 45W) expired on September 30, the “experts” rushed out predictions of an EV sales slowdown in Q4. But, with over 6,800 pages in the Internal Revenue Code still in play, a turbocharged Section 179 tax deduction could still power a strong year for commercial EVs.

The One Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) of 2025 gutted America’s energy independence goals and ensuring its auto industry would fall even further behind the Chinese in the EV race, but the loss of Section 45W wasn’t the only change written into the IRS’ rulebook. Section 179, an immediate expense reduction that business owners can take on depreciable equipment assets, has been made significantly more powerful for 2025.

The section 179 expense deduction is limited to such items as cars, office equipment, business machinery, and computers. This speedy deduction can provide substantial tax relief for business owners who are purchasing startup equipment.

The revised Section 179 tax credit (or, more accurately, expense reduction) allows for a 100% deduction for equipment purchases has doubled to $2.5 million, with a phase-out kicking in at $4 million of capital investments that drops to zero at $6.5 million. That can be applied to new and used vehicles, as well as charging infrastructure, battery energy storage systems, specialized tools, and more (as long as they’re new to you).

“But wait,” as they say. “There’s more!” A revised Section 168(k) also allows for bonus depreciation on eligible equipment and property, accelerating depreciation for a reduced tax burden.

Section 179 and bonus depreciation aren’t mutually exclusive, either, which means that businesses don’t have to exceed the Section 179 spending cap to be able to take advantage of both. A fleet operator can elect to expense a portion of a qualifying vehicle or equipment purchase under Section 179, then apply bonus depreciation to the remaining eligible basis.

With 100% bonus depreciation restored for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, that combination could allow businesses to deduct the entire qualifying business-use cost of an electric truck or other commercial equipment in the first year, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and limitations.

It’s a bit convoluted (what good tax code isn’t?), but these tax incentives are great for businesses looking to buy enough electric equipment assets to exceed the Section 179 spending limit – and, given the new Uber/Tesla semi truck purchase plan, the continued growth of the electric terminal tractor market, and the willingness of several utilities to incentivize both electric commercial vehicles and the deployment of smart EV charging infrastructure, that number may be bigger than you think.

Tax law is weird. Not only are there Federal tax laws and rules that need to be followed, but state and even local county and city rules, as well. As such, you want to make sure they don’t get you the way the got Capone.

Even worse, your favorite journalist (Hi!) is probably an idiot. Get a certified accountant and tax law expert to help walk you through the dirtier details of your specific scenario – but don’t let the complexity of human interaction slow you down, either. The really rich guys you know pay pennies on the tax dollar compared to you and me, because they’re not afraid to ask their accountants for help.

As a tax CPA, I cringe when I see "Sec 179" and the word "credit" put together. It is grossly inaccurate to say that Sec 179 is a tax credit.

Sec 179 and bonus depreciation are nothing new. OBBBA just raised the 179 maximum up, but the deductibility, specifically for heavy vehicles like semis, is unchanged.

The TL;DR version, though, is this: there’s still plenty of incentives out there for fleet operators looking to electrify their operations.

One-off creations can offer several benefits for automakers. For one, they can strengthen a brand’s identity and generate interest, something Bugatti knows well with exclusive hypercars like the Brouillard. Another potential benefit is profitability, as automakers can charge a premium for bespoke vehicles without committing to full-scale production. These creations also cater to the specific demands of clients who typically have exceptionally deep pockets.

Karma Automotive has a new entry into the one-off vehicle space with the Eximius 1. Unveiled at the Concours at Wynn Las Vegas, the Eximius 1 is the first creation under Karma’s new bespoke vehicle program, similar to Porsche’s Sonderwunsch and Rolls-Royce’s Coachbuild. However, the company’s approach is particularly notable because it allows extensive powertrain modifications, not just unique paintwork, body panels, and interiors. For this particular build, the vehicle features a 6.2-liter V8 serving as a generator in a plug-in series hybrid system, a significant departure from the 1.5-liter turbocharged three-cylinder engine used in the Revero donor car.

The Revero is Karma’s outgoing model as it prepares to introduce four new electrified models over the coming years. As such, the Eximius 1 can be seen as a loud send-off following the Revero’s long run dating back to 2016, when it evolved from the Fisker Karma, a luxury plug-in hybrid sedan that fell victim to its manufacturer’s financial collapse.

Karma claims that the track-focused Eximius 1 will produce nearly 1,200 horsepower, attributing 550 hp to the V8 generator and 645 hp to the battery. With that much power on paper, the automaker claims the vehicle will be the most powerful plug-in series hybrid ever developed. It is expected to sprint from zero to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and reach an estimated top speed of over 200 mph. Other performance bits include 21-inch center-lock magnesium wheels, carbon-ceramic brakes with two-piece slotted brake rotors, and Öhlins semi-active suspension.

Finished in Borealis Blue, the one-off vehicle does look like a more aggressive version of the Revero, with modifications like extensive carbon-fiber construction, bodywork that’s 50 mm (1.97 inches) wider, a front splitter, air intakes, and a large rear wing. The cabin, meanwhile, features Recaro carbon-fiber front bucket seats, a simplified carbon-fiber center console with an emergency kill switch, and a specially fitted carbon-fiber racing helmet displayed between the rear seats.

No pricing was disclosed, though Karma said that the Eximius 1 will be delivered to an unnamed customer in 2027.

While the customer gets to drive a vehicle that cannot be found elsewhere, Karma will start to roll out its revitalized series-production lineup, starting with the Gyesera plug-in series hybrid in December 2026. The Amaris GT two-door plug-in series hybrid will arrive in Q4 2027, followed by two EVs, namely the Kaveya, arriving in Q1 2028, and the Ivara, which will follow later. The Kaveya is also planned to use solid-state battery technology.

#4410. Peterbilt makes it easier than ever for government fleets to go electric

Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.

The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5-8 commercial trucks. That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.

“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt. “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”

I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.

See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars (regardless of what you saw on Fox News). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.

Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time, publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.

In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”

Pagani has completed its Huayra 70 trilogy by revealing the Huayra 70 Anima. This unique car joins the other two special editions, marking the end of the founder’s 70th birthday celebration. For fans of manual transmissions, this model includes one as well.

The Huayra 70 series began with the Trionfo, built by Pagani’s Grandi Complicazioni team. Next up was the Huayra 70 Derecho, which showed off at Goodwood earlier this year. This one mixed Pearl Orange with deep Inky Blue for maximum visual drama. But the real headline was under the hood: an 864-horsepower twin-turbo V12 and a seven-speed manual.

Now, the trilogy is complete. Pagani just dropped the Huayra 70 Anima at the Wynn Las Vegas Concours, giving us one last, very different take on the Huayra formula. ‘Anima’ means soul in Italian, and this one definitely has its own vibe.

The Anima stands out with deep metallic blue paint, exposed carbon fiber, and just enough silver and light-blue accents to keep things interesting. It’s an open-top, with sculpted bodywork wrapping the cockpit and roll hoops that look ready for anything.

Up front, the Anima sports a low nose, gaping air intakes, and a splitter that means business. The sides show off wild aero, beefy rear haunches, and a rear wing that refuses to be ignored. Out back, there’s more exposed carbon, an angry diffuser, and a six-pipe exhaust setup that looks ready to wake the neighbors.

Inside, it’s a blue-and-white affair. White leather wraps the seats and most of the cockpit, with blue accents popping up everywhere. Exposed machined aluminum is scattered across the dash, steering wheel, and center console. As always, Pagani’s switchgear is a work of art – every piece looks like it belongs in a jewelry case.

The Anima keeps it old-school with three pedals and a manual shifter, complete with exposed linkage so you can watch the mechanical magic happen. The gear lever matches the blue-and-white theme, and a plaque reminds you this is number 3 of 3 – so don’t expect to see another one at Cars and Coffee.

Pagani’s keeping the Anima’s full specs under wraps for now, but it’s likely packing the same Mercedes-AMG 6.0-liter twin-turbo V12 as the Derecho. That means 864 hp, 811 pound-feet of torque, and all of it going to the rear wheels through a seven-speed manual. We’ll update when Pagani spills more details.

Like its siblings, the Huayra 70 Anima is a one-off, not something you’ll see at your local dealership. Pagani’s Grandi Complicazioni team handled the build, as usual for these ultra-bespoke projects.

No official price yet, but with all the custom work, rare materials, and one-of-one status, you can bet the sticker shock will be real. As for availability, this one’s spoken for, and with Anima rounding out the Huayra 70 trio, don’t expect any more to pop up with this badge.

#4406. Yes, electric motorcycles will replace gasoline motorcycles, but not the way you think

For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.

It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.

But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.

And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.

The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.

For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.

Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.

The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.

You can show someone like that an electric motorcycle with better acceleration, lower maintenance costs, cheaper operating expenses, and the convenience of charging at home, and they still won’t want it.

Not because the electric motorcycle isn’t good enough, but because it isn’t what they love.

And that’s fine. There’s nothing wrong with loving gasoline motorcycles if that’s your thing. But it means that trying to convert those riders may be a losing battle, at least on any meaningful timeline.

Unfortunately though, it seems many years were wasted on that approach. Take Harley-Davidson, for example.

The brand started building its first electric motorcycle over a decade ago – commendable among all the other legacy motorcycle manufacturers that turned their noses up at the thought of going electric. When it was released in 2018, the Harley-Davidson LiveWire received rave reviews, but it just didn’t sell well. For one, it was insanely expensive at $30,000. But the other major reason was that no matter how amazing it was, it wasn’t going to scratch that gasoline itch that most riders still had.

That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line. And this brings us to how electric motorcycles will really replace their gasoline counterparts.

Now consider what’s happening with younger riders today.

Millions of people are growing up riding electric bicycles, electric scooters, and increasingly powerful e-motos. For them, electric two-wheelers aren’t some strange new alternative to the real thing. They are the real thing.

They’ve grown accustomed to instant torque, quiet operation, and the simplicity of twisting a throttle and going. To these riders, a gasoline-powered motorcycle is laughably primitive. It’d be like me handing you a gasoline-powered drill or blender. Yeah, exactly. Now look who’s suddenly on team battery, eh?

So now we have a whole new generation of riders getting ready to come of age. And eventually, many of those riders are going to want something more.

Maybe they’ve spent years riding a 28 mph electric bike, or a 40 mph electric moto. Now they’re young adults, they want to ride on faster roads, and they want something capable of 70 or 80 mph that’s actually street legal. They’ve gone from a sixteen-year-old in a hoodie to a twenty-six-year-old in a collared shirt. Instead of getting to high school, now they’re getting to work. But they haven’t lost that desire to ride.

It’s not because they’ve carefully compared electric and gasoline motorcycles and decided that electric is superior. It’s not because they’re trying to save the planet or reduce their maintenance costs. It’s simply because they grew up with electric two-wheelers as the norm.

It’s simply the next logical step in the type of riding they’ve already been doing for years.

Will a few of them transition over to gasoline-powered motorcycles? Sure. But for most, gasoline motorcycles will never even enter the equation.

Don’t get me wrong, we haven’t seen the last of gasoline motorcycles.

And I don’t even think electric motorcycles are going to suddenly outsell gasoline motorcycles because they become objectively better machines. At least not in the traditional recreational motorcycle markets we’re talking about here.

Instead, I think we’re going to see a somewhat more gradual generational transition.

Today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts will largely keep riding gasoline motorcycles. They’ll keep buying them, maintaining them, and enjoying them for as long as they can.

But as those riders age out of motorcycling, the next generation won’t replace them with another generation of gasoline motorcycle buyers. In other words, gasoline motorcycles will die out with their riders.

Increasingly, those younger riders will have already entered the world of powered two-wheelers through electric bikes and e-motos. When they’re ready to move up, electric motorcycles will be waiting for them.

And over those next few years, the technology will only become better. The only remaining Achilles’ heel of electric motorcycles – their run time – will get better and better as battery technology improves and we move towards solid-state batteries.

Suddenly they’ll be on par with gasoline motorcycles for range and ‘fueling’ time, yet will beat those combustion bikes elsewhere. But at that point, “better” won’t even matter anymore as electrics will be the only comfortable option for the vast majority of new riders. Again, you wouldn’t buy a power drill that runs on a gasoline engine when you’ve seen how convenient and effective a lithium-ion power drill has been your whole life.

Over time, the traditional gasoline motorcycle market will simply shrink as its existing customer base gets older, while electric motorcycles build an entirely new customer base alongside it.

And again, there will be exceptions in both directions. Some lifelong gasoline riders will enthusiastically embrace electric motorcycles, and some younger riders will still discover the appeal of combustion engines and running through the gears.

Living in SE Asia this all sounds very strange. The vast majority of the worlds bikes are not owned as toys, they are the main form of transport for the family. I agree with a lot of the article but Asia is already years ahead. The fuel shortages and sky high prices are pushing people electric far faster than riders are "aging out"

But the broader trend will be driven less by conversion and more by generational replacement.

That’s why electric motorcycles will eventually become the standard, even if they never manage to convince most of today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts to switch.

Gasoline motorcycles won’t necessarily disappear because electric motorcycles finally beat them at their own game. They’ll fade because the next generation of riders will be playing a different game entirely.

In other words, and to paraphrase T. S. Eliot, gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang, but with a whimper.

Owning a Ferrari is special in itself; not many people will ever be able to say that in their lifetime. Because Ferrari recognizes its power as a special brand, it sometimes creates even more desirable models beyond the standard ones. These more special cars usually take inspiration from the past and are sold in limited numbers.

One of the more recent limited-run Ferrari cars is the SP3, built and sold back in 2025 under the “Icona” (Icon) series. These cars have since become ultra-rare and highly sought after, as shown by a recent auction sale.

A very unique SP3 has just sold for an astonishing $18.5 million during the Broad Arrow auction held in Las Vegas. This specific car was Chassis no. 314846 and belonged to a known collector through the Ferrari of Long Island, New York dealership. Only 600 SP3s were ever built, and this is 1 of them, with just 81 miles on the odometer. In terms of design, the SP3 is truly an homage, featuring the patented Ferrari horizontal slats we’ve seen on older cars, but honoring the race cars it’s based on.

The SP3 is already special, but this particular car adds its own twist to stand out even more. It’s finished in a paint palette called Verde Francesca, a lighter shade of green; that option alone costs an additional $42,185. In contrast, the hardtop, lower bodywork trims, splitter, side sills, and trunk lid are painted in glossy carbon fiber. Another key exterior detail that brightens the SP3’s look is the silver-finished rims paired with gloss black brake calipers.

Inside, the SP3 features a two-tone look: some panels use Nero Alcantara upholstery, while the doors and seats feature what Ferrari calls Mustard Aunde Jeans. Behind the driver is the car’s beating heart, a 6.5-liter naturally aspirated V12, producing 829 hp, which is the most powerful road-going engine ever and was derived from the 812 Competizione race car. As expensive as $18 million is, back in 2025 another SP3 sold for much more, at $26 million as the one-of-one 600th example of the limited series.

The SP3’s value and iconic status are also cemented by the inspiration behind the project. It was conceived as “a rolling tribute to one of the marque’s most triumphant afternoons.” In February 1967, Ferrari swept the 24 Hours of Daytona by finishing 1st, 2nd, and 3rd. The cars that achieved it, the 330 P3/P4 and 412P, became the spiritual blueprints for the SP3.

#4404. Eli teases the launch of a much faster electric microcar

Eli Electric Vehicles is getting ready to reveal a new version of its tiny electric microcar, and this one could expand its usefulness beyond the slow lane.

In an Instagram teaser ahead of EICMA in Milan, the company announced the upcoming Eli ZERO MX, describing it as a new L7e vehicle joining its lineup. Eli also teased a special Race Edition, with promotional artwork showing a dark, sporty-looking ZERO with red accents and a visibly open-sided cabin.

The teaser doesn’t give us much to go on in terms of hard and fast details, but the L7e designation is the biggest clue here.

The familiar European Eli ZERO that we test-drove a few years ago is an L6e light quadricycle, with a top speed of 45 km/h (28 mph). Its compact two-seat layout makes it an appealing urban runabout, though that speed ceiling limits its usefulness on faster roads. But L7e vehicles can typically travel at speeds of up to 80-90 km/h (50-56 mph).

A faster version could make the little EV practical for considerably more trips. And there’s already a tantalizing hint: Eli’s Italian website lists an L7e ZERO capable of 85 km/h (53 mph), with a claimed range of up to 200 km (124 miles). Whether those specifications directly describe the upcoming ZERO MX remains unconfirmed by the teaser.

If they do, that would suggest a much more versatile commuter while retaining the tiny footprint that makes these vehicles so easy to park.

I like the idea of a faster LSV, maybe able to cruise at 40 mph. Not a good idea for freeways but suitable for almost all urban and suburban streets. For some a better option than a bike as an urban or second vehicle.

The Race Edition raises a different set of questions. The new vehicle could feature a sportier design, such as race seats and alternative doors. That could point toward a playful or more tuned vehicle, though we’ll have to wait to learn whether “Race” means additional performance or primarily a styling package.

It’s also unclear how closely the Race Edition and ZERO MX are related. The caption presents them separately, while the artwork additionally points towards a second-generation ZERO.

Either way, a roughly 50 mph Eli would be an interesting proposition: still small enough to rethink how much vehicle a daily commute requires, but potentially fast enough to cover routes the original couldn’t comfortably handle.

Eli says the reveal takes place at EICMA, November 3–8, in Hall 22, Stand B40. We’ll be there to see what they unveil.

I-80 between Cheyenne and Laramie, I-70 at the Eisenhower Tunnel and Highway 14 through the Bighorn Mountains are all covered by winter weather advisories Monday across three states.

Ferrari Almost Quit Formula 1, And This $1 Million Pace Car Tells the Story

Inside Doug DeMuro's Secret Underground Car Garage

Snowfall totals vary considerably by elevation, but the highest terrain could pick up 15 inches by Monday night. The National Weather Service also warns of gusts up to 55 mph, slick roads and visibility below a quarter mile in some areas, potentially affecting both Monday commutes.

NWS Cheyenne has a winter weather advisory for the South Laramie Range, including the I-80 summit between Cheyenne and Laramie, from 10 a.m. ET Monday to 1 a.m. ET Tuesday. It calls for 2 to 4 inches of snow in two rounds, one Monday morning and another Monday evening after a lull, with gusts up to 55 mph and reduced visibility during the evening commute.

Farther west on the same interstate, a second advisory covers the North Snowy Range Foothills, including Arlington and Elk Mountain along I-80, from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET Monday. That one forecasts 2 to 4 inches of wet snow and gusts to 40 mph, and the office expects roads, especially bridges and overpasses, to turn slick.

In Colorado, NWS Denver has an advisory above 9,000 feet for the mountains of Summit County, the Mosquito Range and the Indian Peaks, including the Eisenhower Tunnel, Berthoud Pass, Winter Park and Breckenridge. It runs from 7 a.m. ET Monday to 2 a.m. ET Tuesday, with 3 to 7 inches of snow and slippery roads during both Monday commutes.

NWS Billings has the northern Bighorn Mountains in Montana and Wyoming under an advisory until 10 p.m. ET Monday, with up to 10 inches of snow, gusts to 45 mph and the heaviest snow Monday morning. The office warns that snow and blowing snow will make travel along Highway 14 through the range very difficult, with visibility possibly dropping below a quarter mile.

To the south, NWS Riverton expects 6 to 10 inches above 9,000 feet in the southeastern Bighorns from 3 a.m. to 7 p.m. ET Monday, and 10 to 15 inches at the highest elevations near Cloud Peak, with gusts up to 55 mph. Granite Pass could see 5 to 8 inches, while Powder River Pass is forecast for up to 2 inches.

Wyoming’s I-80 summit faces another hazard besides snow: gusts to 55 mph that can put high-profile vehicles at risk of blowing over. The Wyoming Department of Transportation has posted closures for light, high-profile vehicles during wind events since 2011, and in 2023 it began adding specific weights to its blow-over warnings on part of I-80. That lets drivers of trailers and commercial vehicles see whether their load is at risk. Where those signs are not available, the warning reads “Extreme Blow Over Risk.”

WYDOT bases those decisions on current and forecast wind speeds along with the shape of the road, and it has found that blow-over crashes peak in winter, with the most in February and December. Restrictions show up on overhead signs and on the state’s 511 tools.

Drivers heading through the Eisenhower Tunnel should also account for Colorado’s traction law, which the Colorado Department of Transportation applies to I-70 between Dotsero and Morrison from Sept. 1 through May 31.

Compliance means tires with at least 3/16 of an inch of tread plus one of the following: four-wheel or all-wheel drive, tires marked M+S, winter tires with the mountain and snowflake symbol, or tires the manufacturer rates as all-weather. Drivers without any of those need chains or an approved alternative traction device. A standard citation brings a $100 fine plus a surcharge, and the penalty rises to $500 plus a surcharge if the vehicle ends up blocking one or more lanes.

#4401. Battlefield 6 Season 2 delayed like many of us expected, but we're getting a new update and a bonus battle pass path

Battlefield 6 has pushed back its next season by nearly a month in order to refine Season 2 content and implement more of players' feedback.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. #4400. How Europe’s battery passport could have a big impact on US e-bikes

Europe is preparing to introduce a new requirement that could change how electric bicycle batteries are tracked, repaired, recycled, and potentially even resold. Starting in February 2027, new e-bike batteries sold in the European Union will be required to carry a digital battery passport, giving each battery its own digital identity and making important information about its origins and characteristics accessible throughout its lifetime.

And while the rules are European, their impact could eventually reach American e-bike riders, too.

The battery passport requirement comes from the EU’s 2023 Batteries Regulation, which established new standards for battery sustainability, traceability, and transparency. The rules cover several categories of batteries, including those used in electric cars, electric bicycles, electric scooters, and other light electric vehicles.

Beginning February 18, 2027, newly placed batteries in these categories will need digital passports accessible through QR codes. Scanning the code will provide access to information about the battery, though exactly what users can see will depend on their authorization level.

The information can include details such as the battery’s manufacturer, chemistry, capacity, cycle count, carbon footprint, and materials used in its construction. The system also provides for information about battery performance and durability, including data related to battery health and degradation.

That last part could be particularly interesting for electric bicycle owners.

Anyone who has purchased a used electric bicycle knows that the battery is often one of the biggest unknowns. A bike might look nearly new, but its battery could have hundreds of charge cycles under its belt and significantly reduced capacity.

Even a quick test ride before a secondhand e-bike purchase may fail to demonstrate just how little capacity remains in a heavily used battery.

With replacement e-bike batteries costing hundreds of dollars, that’s a pretty important detail.

The battery passport system could eventually help address that problem by making battery information more transparent. However, there’s an important distinction: the regulations don’t necessarily guarantee that everyday consumers will be able to scan a QR code and immediately see a battery’s remaining health percentage. Some of that information may be restricted to authorized users.

Even so, the system could help repair shops, recyclers, and secondhand buyers better understand the batteries they’re dealing with.

It could also make life more complicated for e-bike manufacturers, especially smaller brands that will now need to ensure their batteries meet the new documentation and traceability requirements.

There’s currently no equivalent nationwide battery passport requirement for electric bicycles in the United States, but that doesn’t mean American riders won’t eventually benefit.

Many major e-bike manufacturers sell their products in both Europe and North America. US-based companies like Trek and Specialized have major markets in Europe, and will have to comply with the new law. Chinese companies and other Asian manufacturers will also need to produce compliant batteries. Once those companies have developed systems to track individual batteries and provide digital passports for their European products, they may find it easier to extend those systems to their American models rather than maintain entirely separate processes.

That doesn’t mean US-bound batteries will automatically receive passports, but it could create an interesting spillover effect.

And considering how expensive e-bike batteries can be, anything that makes it easier to understand their condition, verify their origins, or facilitate repairs could be a welcome development.

For now, Europe is leading the charge on battery transparency. But if the system proves useful, American e-bike riders might eventually get some of the same benefits without waiting for Washington to catch up.

An engine replacement and a new front differential were supposedly in order for this Toyota Tundra. A closer inspection, however, painted a different picture.

If you’re trying to stay within a budget every time your car needs work, independent repair shops can be heaven-sent. Unlike dealerships with their pricing rituals, independent mechanics often give you a fighting chance to fix your ride without spending a fortune.

However, not every shop sees things the same way. That’s why it’s always smart to get a second opinion before you green-light any wallet-busting repairs.

One Toyota Tundra owner learned this lesson the hard way. He took his truck in for a pre-road trip checkup and got hit with a repair estimate so steep it practically begged for a second opinion.

The vehicle in question was a 2016 Toyota Tundra with approximately 118,000 miles. According to the original shop’s assessment, the truck supposedly needed a replacement engine because of leaking head gaskets and valve covers. It also needed a front differential carrier assembly, with the estimate for the latter reportedly reaching $5,700. The combined bill came close to $25,000.

Enter Dave of Dave’s Auto Center, the second-opinion mechanic. He wasn’t buying it. The Tundra rolled into his shop under its own power, the engine sounded happy, and the oil level was right where it should be. No major oil or coolant leaks in sight, either.

Then there was the front CV axle. The first shop said it had too much play and needed a whole new front differential assembly. Dave? He couldn’t even get the problem to show up at first.

During a four-wheel-drive test, he eventually traced the metallic scraping noise to a slightly bent dust shield. A quick adjustment with a screwdriver stopped the noise.

He also contacted the original shop to discuss its findings, although the disagreement over the axle’s condition remained unresolved pending a more precise measurement.

After speaking with the customer, Dave concluded that the truck didn’t need an engine or front differential replacement. Instead, it needed overdue preventive maintenance, including fresh fluids and spark plugs.

He also planned to have his technicians measure the axle’s movement using a dial indicator to establish whether the play was actually excessive.

There are a few takeaways here for car owners. First, don’t automatically approve expensive repairs simply because they’re listed on an inspection report. Ask for supporting evidence, photographs, measurements, and an explanation of why a particular component needs replacement.

Second, pay attention to your vehicle’s symptoms. A truck that runs normally, doesn’t overheat, and isn’t losing coolant may warrant further investigation before an engine replacement is considered.

Finally, don’t underestimate the value of a second opinion. In this case, a customer potentially avoided a nearly $25,000 repair bill simply by having another mechanic take a closer look.

Average gas car lasts ~150k miles. For sure requiring more maintenance to reach that mileage than an EV. Achieving ~500k on the original motor and over 300k on a battery is quite impressive.

Look forward to hitting 200k and beyond in each. For the first time in over 30 years of driving, I don’t look forward to replacing our cars as they get over 100k miles - rather I look forward to the next 100k miles of driving.

Out of Spec Renew replaced the 2019’s battery pack that was experiencing serious battery faults and cell-voltage imbalances with a stable, lower-mile example from a 2017 model. #4397. Shaquille O’Neal Bought This 2004 Rolls-Royce Phantom Just to Prove a Point

It’s now for sale on Bring a Trailer. Maybe you’ve got something to prove?

One of the greatest basketball players of all time, four-time NBA champion Shaquille O’Neal was one of the most formidable centers in the game. That doesn’t mean he never got outplayed.

To hear him tell the story, during his stint playing for the Lakers, he wandered into a Rolls-Royce dealership dressed casually in sweats. In his words, “I like to spend money, but I don’t like to waste money. I don’t want to spend $400,000 for a car.” Thus, every time the salesman tells him the price for a particular Roller, O'Neal waves him off.

Finally, the salesman asks, “You’re asking about all these cars—can you afford them?” Riled up, Shaq buys three Rolls-Royces on the spot. Heck of a flex by the NBA player, but not a bad move by the salesman, who gets to pocket a triple-Rolls commission.

See all results for used cars for sale near 28625

One of that trio of Rolls-Royces just turned up at Bring a Trailer (which, like Car and Driver, is part of Hearst Autos): a 2004 Phantom sedan in glossy silver. Yes, the driver’s seat goes back, way back, but this Roller is going to set you back far less than O’Neal’s impulse purchase.

This was the debut model year for the Phantom VII, the first Rolls-Royce of the BMW ownership era. Like Shaq, much of this generation of Rolls-Royce’s curb presence comes from its sheer size; the sedan was longer than a Ford Excursion when it launched.

Power came from an enlarged version of the BMW 750’s V-12, here displacing 6.75 liters. Peak power was 453 horsepower, but a more subtle motivating force was the 531 pound-feet of torque. Almost 400 pound-feet was available from just 1000 rpm, fed through a smooth-shifting six-speed automatic, giving the Phantom a driving experience less like a luxury sedan and more like a Cunard cruise liner.

Add in coach doors with integrated umbrellas, self-righting Rolls-Royce center-caps on the wheels, and a retractable Spirit of Ecstasy on the massive hood, and this generation of Phantom is plenty imposing. It’s even better on the inside, with acres of walnut trim, buttery leather, and deep-pile lambswool carpets. Other faintly ridiculous amenities include rear picnic tables and six-zone climate control.

Shaq says he barely drove his three Rolls-Royces, although this example now has 45K miles on the odometer. That means there’s still plenty of luxurious life ahead, along with a great story about the day somebody scored on Shaquille O’Neal.

Used electric cars now find buyers nearly two weeks sooner than used gas cars, according to a new iSeeCars analysis of more than 1.5 million one- to five-year-old vehicles. The average used EV sells in 41.9 days, while a gas model needs 54.8.

Tesla would seem the obvious leader, since three of its models rank among the five used cars with the biggest price increases over the past year. It isn’t. The fastest-selling used EV is an Audi that typically finds a buyer in under a month, no Tesla appears in the top 10, and a Toyota bZ4X and a Honda Prologue both sell faster than any Tesla in the study. The full ranking also shows a clear pattern: compact and midsize crossovers fill the top of the list, while large SUVs and pickups sit far longer.

The average used EV now sells in 41.9 days, down from 46.6 a year earlier, according to the iSeeCars study, while gas vehicles slowed from 45.7 days to 54.8. Used EV prices rose 9.8% over the same period to an average of $32,533, which now puts them $579 above the average used gas car.

iSeeCars links the shift to fuel costs, and gas prices line up with that: regular gasoline averaged $4.33 a gallon in September, the highest September average on record, according to AAA.

Used EV Prices Jump Nearly 10% After Years of Declines

Used electric vehicle prices have reversed course, climbing nearly 10% as budget-conscious buyers flock to the secondary market for affordable options.

The Audi Q4 Sportback e-tron is the fastest-selling used EV at 29.8 days, quick enough to rank third among all used vehicles. The Toyota bZ4X follows at 33.3 days, the Lexus RZ 300e at 34.3, the Honda Prologue at 35.0 and the standard Audi Q4 e-tron at 35.8. The Kia EV6, BMW i4 and Chevrolet Equinox EV share 10th place at 36.7 days.

Tesla shows up on a different list entirely. The Model S rose 22.5% to $57,862, the Model X 18.0% to $61,309 and the Model 3 15.4% to $28,931, making them three of the five used cars with the biggest annual price increases. iSeeCars does not publish how long a used Tesla takes to sell, only that none ranks in the EV top 10. Buyers are paying more for used Teslas, but the listings disappearing quickest belong to other brands.

Grouped by body style and size, the ten fastest- and ten slowest-selling used EVs split cleanly. All mainstream compact and midsize crossovers on the two lists appear among the fastest sellers, while all large SUVs and full-size pickups fall among the slowest.

Source: iSeeCars, 1- to 5-year-old used vehicles, September 2026. Segment groupings by body style and size; iSeeCars does not group models by segment. Used EV average: 41.9 days. The electric Dodge Charger (80.1 days) also ranks among the slowest.

The clearest example comes from a single automaker. A used Equinox EV sells in 36.7 days, while a used Silverado EV takes 89.1, nearly two and a half times as long, and the Cadillac Escalade IQ is the slowest-selling used EV in the study at 128.7 days. Six of the ten slowest-selling used EVs come from GM.

Luxury models break the pattern. The Q4 Sportback e-tron and the Cadillac Optiq are both compact luxury crossovers, yet the Audi sells in 29.8 days and the Cadillac takes more than twice as long. Why individual models land where they do is something the data doesn’t answer.

For anyone hunting used EV deals, the ranking offers different takeaways depending on what kind of EV you’re shopping for.

If you want a compact or midsize electric crossover, expect competition. A used Equinox EV, bZ4X, Prologue, EV6 or Q4 e-tron typically sells in about a month, and with used EV prices up 9.8% over the past year, buyers shouldn’t assume these models will become cheaper simply by waiting.

If you need an electric pickup or a large SUV, you can take your time. A used Silverado EV, Sierra EV or Escalade IQ stays on the market for roughly three to four months on average, which leaves room to compare listings before committing.

If you have your heart set on a Tesla, you are shopping the used EVs with the steepest price increases. The Model 3 still averages $28,931, below the $32,533 used EV average, but that figure is 15.4% higher than a year ago, and the Model S and Model X have climbed even more.

Tesla’s used prices are rising faster than almost anything else on the market, yet in the race for buyers, Toyota, Audi and Honda are getting there first.

#4394. Bestselling US e-bike Lectric XP4 relaunched in limited-edition with new colors and gear

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.

Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.

The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green). Each is priced at $1,399 and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.

So while the underlying bike remains largely unchanged from the bones of the XP 750, the new packages are designed to make the XP4 even more useful straight out of the box.

The District edition is aimed squarely at urban commuters, sporting a stealthy Matte Black finish and an accessory package designed for daily transportation.

That includes two waterproof pannier bags, a redesigned LevelUp rear cargo rack, a heavy-duty bike lock, and an upgraded high-output headlight. There’s also a fast charger, suspension seat post with comfort saddle, and handlebar phone mount.

It’s essentially a ready-made commuter setup, particularly for riders looking to replace some of their car trips with an e-bike.

The Jubilee edition takes a more casual approach, arriving in a distinctive Matte Thistle colorway. Designed for neighborhood cruising, weekend errands, and trips to the local farmers market, it swaps the commuter-focused panniers for a front and rear cargo package and a small roll-top bag.

It also includes the upgraded headlight, lock, fast charger, suspension seat post, comfort saddle, and phone mount.

Finally, the Ridge edition is built for riders who prefer their adventures a bit farther from the pavement.

Finished in Matte Forest green, the Ridge comes with front and rear cargo accessories for carrying outdoor gear, plus a fishing rod holder on the High-Step version. The Step-Thru model instead receives a weather-resistant roll-top bag.

Like the other two editions, the Ridge also includes the upgraded lighting, lock, charger, and comfort accessories.

“We wanted to deliver ready-made, purpose-built setups that empower our community to jump on and ride without having to configure their gear from scratch,” explained Lectric co-founder and CEO Levi Conlow.

Conlow also seems particularly proud of the new finishes, calling them the three best paint jobs Lectric has produced in its seven-year history.

While the new colors and accessory bundles are the main attraction, the bikes retain the same core features that helped make the XP4 such a popular choice.

That includes Lectric’s in-house developed dynamic torque sensor, which measures how hard the rider pedals to deliver a more natural-feeling electric assist experience.

The bikes also feature hydraulic disc brakes, an 8-speed Shimano Altus drivetrain, and a full-color TFT display.

As with the standard XP4, riders get the familiar folding frame design, integrated turn signals and brake lights, and 20-inch puncture-resistant mixed-terrain tires.

All three limited editions are available in both High-Step and Step-Thru frame configurations.

At $1,399, the new models aren’t trying to reinvent the XP4 formula. Instead, they’re offering a more fully equipped version of a bike that has already proven itself with American riders.

And that’s probably a smart move. Lectric has built its reputation on delivering an impressive amount of e-bike for the money, and bundling useful accessories into a relatively affordable package plays right into that strategy.

The limited-edition models are available now, though Lectric says quantities are strictly limited.

For riders who have been considering an XP4 but wanted something a bit more distinctive than the standard colors, these new editions could be a compelling reason to finally pull the trigger.

And for those looking to score an even better deal, Lectric has also officially kicked off its Black Friday sale.

The company is calling it its biggest sale of the year, with some of its lowest prices ever and discounts of up to $800 across its lineup.

So whether you’re eyeing one of the new limited-edition XP4 models or another e-bike in Lectric’s extensive catalog, now could be a particularly good time to buy.
