#4393. Upward Mobility: 1997 $30K Luxury Sedans Compared

Nine ways—Acura 3.2TL, Cadillac Catera, Ford Taurus SHO, Infiniti I30, Lexus ES300, Mazda Millenia, Mitsubishi Diamante, Saab 900SE, Volvo 850GLT—to express yourself on the way to the top.

From the February 1997 issue of Car and Driver.

Let’s say your corporate star is rising. Your cozy cubicle has been swapped for an office with floor-to-ceiling walls and a door. Your annual salary just achieved that magic sixth digit. The paint is drying on your first personalized parking space. Now the question is, what are you going to park on that providential piece of pavement?

You’ve worked hard and earned the right to drive something special. You want to make a statement about who you are and where you’re headed, but you must choose wisely. From time to time, you’ll be the designated driver shuttling your foursome from the three-martini lunch to the links, so a sports car is out. Your spouse already drives a sport-utility vehicle, so a sedan it must be. It would be impolitic to outzoot the boss with a flashier car, so you’ll be shopping in the “near luxury” segment.

Prepare to spend more than the cost of the fanciest family cars that top out around $28,000 but don’t cross the luxury-tax threshold of $34,000. This way you’ll send the message that you’re a good ol' fiscal conservative, anti-tax type.

See all results for used cars for sale near 02777

Our Buyers Guide lists 17 sedans in that price range. We eliminated five of those based on prior com­parison-test standings and road-test results. We excluded the BMW 3-series and the Mercedes C-class because reason­ably equipped models only evade the luxury tax in four-cylinder guise and their subcompact interior dimensions make them less suitable transportation for four corporate execs. That last argument also ruled out the lovely Audi A4. The remaining nine cars are the cream of this crop. Each should easily satisfy the middle man­ager’s needs and caprices.

Since we last evaluated this class in August 1994, the Acura TL, the Cadillac Catera, and the Infiniti I30 have joined the seg­ment. The Ford Taurus SHO sprouted a V-8, lost its manual trans­mission, and was recast as—in Ford’s words—an “executive express.” The Lexus ES300 and the Mitsubishi Diamante have been redesigned, the Volvo 850GLT has been given a new light-pressure turbocharged engine, and the Saab 900SE V-6 was promoted into our price range. The Mazda Millenia S, with its supercharged Miller-cycle engine, has drifted up in price, so we invited the normally aspirated L model instead.

The field includes seven 24-valve V-6 engines, one turbocharged five-­cylinder, and a 32-valve V-8. Each spins through a four-speed automatic trans­mission (only Infiniti offers a stick). There are two Swedes, one true Yank, one German/Yank (the Opel-derived Cadillac), and five Japanese in the bunch. Each speaks with a slightly different accent of luxury, style, and class.

In straight-line acceleration, the pack ­is remarkably tight—seven of the nine cars perform within 0.3 second of the average 0-to-60-mph and quarter-mile times. Handling behavior varies more widely, as does each manufacturer’s interpretation of luxury equipment.

See all results for used cars for sale near 02777

Although none of these cars is spartan, none is fully loaded, either. For example, not one car in this group is equipped with all four of these less-than-exotic items: traction control, a CD player, remote key­less entry, and variable intermittent wipers. Only three have heated seats. Just two have dual-zone climate controls. The Saab alone has a trip computer.

To fully appreciate the subtle person­ality traits of these nine middle-manage­ment-grade luxo-cruisers, we headed for the Hocking Hills of southeast Ohio. Here's how the cars stacked up.

For those climbing the corporate ladder at an avant-garde corporation, the Saab 900SE is a must-have. It fairly screams “I’m different and proud of it” to parking­ lot passersby. From its quirky ignition switch on the floor to its unmistakable shape to its tall-dining-room-chair front seats, this is the car with its baseball cap on backward.

Some of the 900’s quirks are quite useful, like the rear hatch and the split-folding back seat (with armrest pass­through) that, when folded, allows this car to swallow more than 50 cubic feet of cargo or a box measuring, in inches, 62 by 34 by 25. Other quirks are less endearing, like the upright, far-away, 747-style wind­shield that limits the view of overhead traffic lights.

The 900SE also has one of the smallest and least comfortable rear seats. Its low cushion provides Viking-scale headroom at the expense of thigh support and legroom. On the upside, there are three shoulder belts in back, each of which has a lever on the latch that allows the lap belt to be cinched tight for child­-seat installation or for restraining riders during exu­berant driving.

Our Saab cast the smallest shadow of any car in this group, and it racked up the highest skidpad grip (0.81 g, tied with the Mazda) and the best braking performance (168 feet from 70 mph). But a lack of road feel through the steering and considerable understeer conspired with the 2.5-liter V-6’s lack of low-end grunt to limit the Saab’s ability to generate grins out in the twisties.

The 900SE comes equipped with crea­ture comforts like heated power seats with three-position memory, rear-seat air vents, an eight-function trip computer, and a sporting traction-control system that doesn’t slow the car down as much as other systems do. But the interior looks plasticky, and noise levels are the highest of the bunch. Its jiggly, coarse ride ranks just above that of the roughrider Taurus.

HIGHS: High-capacity hatchback design, superb brakes, bags of character.LOWS: Lack of low-end punch, cramped back seat.VERDICT: The round peg in a square-hole segment.

Saab’s near-luxury formula is harder edged and less refined than its competitors’. We think that approach better suits those 900 models priced in the twenties.

From the backward baseball cap, we turn to the navy pinstripe suit. The Acura 3.2TL is the corporate yes man of this bunch. From its anonymous but handsome exterior to its mid­pack-performing engine and chassis to its well-appointed, conservative interior, this car meets, but never exceeds, the minimal requirements spelled out in its job description.

The TL drew its loudest praise during the highway slog down to southern Ohio. Editors lauded its low-cowl visibility, its smooth ride on the freeway, its rich-looking gath­ered leather and reasonably convincing fake-wood interior trim, and its impeccable Japanese build quality. There was some grumbling about the coarseness of its aging 3.2-liter V-6 and the transmission’s tendency to hunt for gears and select them sharply, but there was unanimous praise for the slalom­-gate shifter.

Unfortunately, that Germanic shifter suggests a sporting demeanor that the rest of the car doesn’t support. For starters, it seemed impossible to get completely comfortable in the driver’s seat because there is no place to rest one’s left foot. The plastic dead pedal is positioned more than four inches far­ther away than the accelerator, which puts it out of reach. The steering feels numb on center and then turns in sharply without delivering much road feel. The tires offer just 0.76 g of grip, the lowest of the group (tied with the Lexus). The TL’s smooth ride is offset by a lack of rebound control when the going gets rough. “Wow, I start driving like a little old lady in this car,” said one ordinarily enthusiastic driver.

Super-slab cruising is the TL’s forte, but it’s not the class leader in that category, either. Rear-seat com­fort is compromised by a low cushion and uncomfortable armrests. Engine noise is on the high end of the range in this class, and the 14- cubic-foot trunk is narrow in back with many intrusions to pack around.

HIGHS: Smooth, syrupy freeway ride; gated shifter; rich interior appointments.LOWS Legs-akimbo driving position, coarse engine, underdamped chassis. VERDICT: The Waylon Smithers of the group—eager to please, unable to excite.

We prefer cars that show a bit more initiative. Acura’s agreeable, play-it-safe TL sends the wrong message from our parking space.

This burly brute in its athletic­-cut Armani seems just a bit out of place in this group—as if its rise to power may have involved a little rough stuff. The Taurus SHO is the longest and widest car here, and it’s motivated by the only V-8 engine.

That engine is largely respon­sible for transforming the pure­bred, hard-nosed sport-sedan SHO of old into today’s gentrified “executive express.” Trouble is, that transformation is not com­plete. The smooth and sonorous V-8, although less potent than the old V-6, is quite competitive in this class. It’s the interior and chassis that need a promotion to executive grade.

Five fit comfortably on-board, but the stark monochrome inte­rior offers no suggestions that the car is at all special. The texture of the plastic dash-and-door trim resembles, well, plastic. New leather bucket seats provide good lateral support, especially at shoulder level, but they look inexpensive.

The chassis tuning is classic American sporty—lots of roll con­trol with rock-hard bushings that telegraph small-bump harshness, and softened springs to swallow the big stuff. “I didn’t know the road was so bumpy until I drove this car,” wrote one of us, who later lamented a Rice Krispies-like chorus of interior squeaks and creaks elicited by the harsh ride. Sadly, that harshness doesn’t pay off in superla­tive handling. Although it corners flatly with 0.80 g of grip, the SHO’s large size makes it a bit unwieldy on winding roads and in our emergency lane-change maneuver.

The engine, despite its eager note, is peaky by nature. There’s too little torque on tap at low revs, and overly tall gearing makes it slow to rev. In almost every acceleration test, the five-cylinder Volvo 850GLT trounced the SHO. And yet, predictably, the SHO’s fuel economy on this trip—18 mpg—was the group’s worst.

HIGHS: Unmistakable V-8 burble, big interior, lots of car for the money.LOWS: Low-buck interior, peaky engine, punishing ride.VERDICT: A ruffian among Rhode scholars.

The SHO sports the most fiscally pru­dent price in the group ($30,585), but it needs a Dale Carnegie course to round out its personality before it earns true “exec express” status.

Just beneath the chrome façade of this luxo-cruiser lies the honest middle-class values of a two-time Ten Best-winning Nissan Maxima. We’ve always been fond of Nissan’s lively 3.0-liter V-6 and its crisp, responsive steering, so we expected the I30 to impress us in this comparison.

In the corporate climb from family car to near-luxo status symbol, the Maxima gains a number of standard power acces­sories, a terrific Bose audio system with CD player, a softened suspension, and styling upgrades inside and out.

Parked alongside its competitors, the I30’s exterior looks gussied up and lacks the cohesive and clean beauty of the ES300 and the Diamante. The interior upgrades are more successful. Gathered leather on the seats and doors and respectable-looking faux-wood trim befit a car competing in this class. The seats are quite comfortable, although the rear seat­back is reclined a bit more than we like.

The V-6 achieves average acceleration and above-average fuel economy with the tallest gearing in this group. The softened suspension smooths out one-wheel bumps admirably, but when two wheels thwack an expansion joint at the same time, the seat and the steering wheel rever­berate, revealing this Infiniti’s humble family-car roots. Increased pitch, dive, and roll combine with howling tires to sap the fun out of twisty-road running (and they drop the I30 to last place in our lane-change test).

A $2200 Touring package buys trac­tion control, a limited-slip differential, bigger tires, and sport-suspension tuning. So equipped, an I30 might have fared better in this test, but none was available at test time.

HIGHS: Quiet, comfortable interior; low price.LOWS: Overly gussied-up exterior, weak-kneed suspension.VERDICT: A middle-of-­the-road middle-manager’s machine.

At $30,795, our I30 was equipped with heated seats, an integrated garage­-door opener, and remote-control one-­touch lowering of all four windows. But the I30’s jack-of-all-trades, master-of­-none demeanor makes a loaded Maxima SE look like the better buy. We wonder then, was the Maxima’s promotion to this class a textbook example of the Peter Prin­ciple at work?

Mazda’s Millenia has an “old money” patrician feel about it. Originally intended to spearhead Mazda’s aborted Amati line of high-end cars, its build quality, panel fits, and freedom from vibration, squeaks, and rattles are world-class. The body has a graceful and balanced look with a low, broad stance on the road. Such presence!

Inside, some editors carped about the almost military appearance of the dark-colored dash, but the material quality and the attention to detail are nonpareil. To wit: Carpeting lines the sides of the front seat cushions where leather might otherwise chafe against plastic to make noise. It’s well equipped, too, with traction control and heated seats and the group’s only infi­nitely adjustable electric tilting steering wheel. Of course, with a price that tiptoes into luxo-tax land at $34,049, it should be loaded. The rear seat, however, offers too little thigh support, no toe room, and uncomfortable armrests.

Ride and handling are bal­anced expertly. The Mil­lenia’s steering provides a strong sense of straight-ahead and excellent road feel. The chassis clings to the road with 0.81 g of grip, which ties with the Saab for top honors. Best of all, the ride quality doesn’t suffer—most road imperfections are heard more than they are felt.

So why is this limber aris­tocrat warming the fifth-place podium? Mainly because its 170-horse 2.5-liter engine is hopelessly outgunned here. “Definitely works overtime to make power, and it still comes up short,” said one tester. Its 9.2-second acceleration to 60 mph was almost a second slower than every other car, and its 6.1-second 50-to-70-mph passing time kept the Millenia trapped behind trucks on two-lane high­ways, while its driver waited impatiently for extra-wide passing gaps.

HIGHS: Build quality, chassis dynamics, Mazda rarity.LOWS: Overworked, underfed engine; uncomfortable rear-seat cushion.VERDICT: A charm-school graduate that needs to head for the gym.

Those who are smitten by the Mil­lenia’s chassis charms and its low-volume cachet might want to wait for another pro­motion and buy the $37,289 Miller-engined Millenia S (unless the boss already drives one).

Cadillac’s near-luxo nominee comes with a fresh green card and a thick German accent, although it’s gone shopping at Men’s Wearhouse for a Yankee wardrobe. We think it should have kept the Deutsche duds, but beneath the cluttered and cliched exterior lies a true autobahn stormer.

Editors filled the logbook with glow­ing praise about the Catera’s secure, stable, and well-weighted steering, its firm brakes, and the neutral handling demeanor of this group’s only rear-drive entrant. Classic Teutonic body rigidity helps this Cadillac absorb bumps with a single audible thunk and no reverberations. It has a Euro-firm but supple ride.

The Catera weighs in at 3794 pounds—the heaviest car here by 264 pounds—so it was not the quickest car on our handling loop. But its superb chassis control inspired a level of confidence that few of these cars could match.

A variable-resonance intake system broadens the 3.0-liter V-6’s torque curve substantially, so the Catera runs rings around the Mil­lenia (with which it shares a disad­vantageous weight-to-power ratio of 19 pounds per horsepower), despite having taller gearing.

Inside, the tall, chair-like seats—­front and back—drew praise for their lateral support and, again, Teutonic headroom. The Catera’s continental switchgear was viewed by many as subpar in refinement and ergonomic functionality, how­ever, and the European cigarette­-lighter socket is too large to fit American accessory plugs. Our Volvo has an Amer­ican lighter—why doesn’t the Cadillac?

The two-tone-gray dash is busy and button-encrusted, but then our $33,635 base Catera was adorned with more fea­tures and amenities than any of its com­petitors, including dual-zone climate con­trols with rear-seat vents, automatic headlamps, one-touch-down windows all around, and steering-wheel radio controls.

HIGHS: Stable, confident ride and handling on the autobahn as well as on our “Hockingheim” circuit.LOWS: Out-of-fashion exterior, excessive avoirdupois, low-grade Euro-switchgear.VERDICT A German athlete in need of a diet and a makeover.

The Catera is a strong contender in this class. Its eccentricities are mostly charming. To reach the head of this class, it needs to lose some weight and update its wardrobe.

This multinational player was con­ceived in Japan and born in Australia, but it speaks fluent Luxury with a perfect American accent. Check the stats: biggest interior with the most comfortable back seat, biggest-displacement engine making the most torque. Now check the ratings sheet: top marks in the ride and comfort—­and styling—categories.

The interior trim, in rich contrasting hues of butterscotch and mocha, also sug­gests an American heritage, especially the center console, which is slathered with too much fake wood. Still, the front and rear seats afford stretch-out room that only the Taurus can match, and the Diamante’s seat cushions are a model for the class. The armrests are all properly positioned and comfortable—it’s a little thing, but one that none of the others managed to get right. In back, there is ample room for toes knees, heads, and three sets of shoul­ders combined with a better view out than in the SHO. Throw in adjustable rear-seat headrests, front and rear reading lamps, and a comfortable shoulder belt for the center rear seat, and it’s easy to see why we deemed this the only true New York-to-L.A. back seat of the bunch.

Those who set out on such a journey will appreciate the Dia­mante’s class-leading interior quietness and its ride-tuned sus­pension, which fairly smothers all manner of road imperfections.

The driver will also appreciate the Diamante V-6’s 231 pound­-feet of torque, which propel this big boy off the line, out of tight corners, and around slower traffic quickly and without breathing hard.

But when the road turns twisty, get out the Dramamine. That smooth-riding suspension rolls over and plays dead when pushed. Howling understeer on the handling loop brought sweat to the brow of one editor, prompting this logbook entry: “It’s like the steering and the sus­pension haven’t been introduced.”

HIGHS: Pressed and creased styling; gorgeous, cavernous interior; torquey V-6.LOWS: Floats and corners like a traditional Yankee land yacht.VERDICT: The long-haul cruiser of this bunch.

The globe-trotting Diamante needs to spend some time studying road manners in Europe. For now, it’s a terrific luxo-cruiser on the American plan.

Meet the come-from-behind go-getter of the group. Volvo’s new light-pressure turbocharger transforms the 850 from a coarse, unrefined, and underpowered also-ran to the bullet-train of this class. Five cars can best its 190 horsepower, and six can out-twist its 191 pound-feet of torque, but a tiny turbo that spools up instantly provides max torque at a low, low 1800 rpm.

Mounted in a 3188-pound box, that translates to range-topping scoot: 0 to 60 mph in 7.0 seconds, the quarter-mile in 15.4 seconds at 91 mph, and passing times that are roughly a half-second ahead of the pack. And this acceleration arrives smoothly, without the neck-snapping boost of the full-blown Volvo turbos.

But this is no one-trick pony. It also squirts around twisty roads with elan. Its scrappy little Michelin MXV4s hang on with stoic silence right up to their 0.79-g limit, while the cloth seats grip the driver. The steering and the brakes are linear and communicative, and that mighty-mite motor champs at the bit at every apex.

Ride quality suffers little in the name of handling. The tires and the bushings absorb most sharp impacts, and the body structure—it exceeds the rigidity of any other 850 we’ve driven, although no struc­tural enhancements have been publi­cized for 1997—absorbs the big bumps with minimal fuss.

The passenger cube provides rea­sonable space and comfort for four or five occupants, each of whom gets a shoulder belt and a headrest, and there are side airbags in front. The rear seats fold independently, and the front pas­senger seat also folds forward for car­rying long objects. The interior is not as rich-looking as some, although leather seats ($1195) and a wood dash ($810) are options. Still, our $32,330 850GLT was equipped with most of what a mid­grade exec needs—except traction control, which adds $325.

HIGHS: Bullet-train performance and handling; safe, comfortable interior.LOWS: Even the exhaust pipe is square.VERDICT: The Norse god of executive transport, with a face only a Swede could love.

Two things kept this perfor­mance champ from grabbing the brass ring: Its Eighties cubist styling (“Goes like stink, with looks to match,” quipped one smart aleck) and past experience with far less robust 850s, which concerned us that this one might be a ringer.

You know the fair-haired, golden-boy Dudley Doright type at the office that everyone loves to hate? The ES300 is that guy. Cultured, athletic, suave, good­looking—the Lexus won top marks in eight of our 13 voting categories. We suspect the other cars were sneering at this one when no one was looking.

Every inch of the ES300 looks expensive, from its wind-chis­eled, two-tone exterior to its leather- and genuine-wood­-trimmed interior. Even the plastic panels look and feel like leather.

At $33,822, our test car lacked traction control, heated seats, and a CD player, but the entry-­level Lexus’s ability to do everything well so impressed us that it took top honors in the value category.

The ES300’s 200-horse 3.0-liter V-6 and four-speed automatic trans­mission established the class bench­mark for smoothness and delivered 60-mph, quarter-mile, and passing acceleration times within a couple tenths of the V-8-powered SHO’s.

In the chassis department, a new, cockpit-adjustable suspension al­lowed the ES300 to tie the Diamante’s top score in ride and match the Volvo’s winning scores in the handling and fun-to-drive categories. Set to “Sport,” the shocks help limit body roll and maintain optimal tire contact with the road in quick maneu­vers like our emergency lane change. The ES300 took a 4-mph lead over the Volvo in that test, despite wearing the least-grippy tires in the group.

Set to “Comfort,” the chassis absorbs large bumps and dips grace­fully, with a bit more float. Firmer bushings in the Lexus give the Dia­mante an advantage over small irreg­ularities, however.

A two-inch wheelbase stretch for 1997 has improved rear-seat comfort, especially with three passengers in back, by reducing wheelhouse intru­sion. But the new, slimmer sunroof design still compromises headroom somewhat.

HIGHS: Dream Whip drivetrain, Ritz-Carlton interior, Swiss-Army suspension.LOWS: Missing a few key features.VERDICT: An overachiever that does almost everything well.

Is the ES300 the perfect car in this segment? No. For that we’d need to hold the price and add the Cadillac’s features, the Diamante’s back seat, and the Volvo’s turbo. But its com­prehensive competence sends the message we’d want delivered from our personalized parking spot.

#4392. Electric trucks hit 50% of China’s heavy truck sales, diesel demand falls

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.

And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.

In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.

December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.

Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.

That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.

It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.

CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.

Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.

CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy.

The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.

For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.

Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.

So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.

China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.

2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.

Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.

There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.

Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.

A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.

The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE, which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.

Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.

This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.

Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.

And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.

The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

China having a lot of phev and EV vehicles has helped with oil pricing around the world, more notably in the current american-caused oil crisis. It would be worse if they were all traditional powered cars and trucks.

Now to be clear, I'm not saying that it has made a massive impact or is even the only reason why the oil crisis isn't much worse, it's just one of a few steps China made to reduce the impact of the oil crisis. But going electric everywhere we can has a stabilizing effect when oil shocks show up

Europe at least has the regulation, and its best markets, at 10% to 24%, are roughly where China was in 2024 and 2025.

The question now is how long Chinese truck makers stay home. SANY and BYD already sell electric trucks in Europe, and CATL is building the swap network for them. If those trucks can come close to China’s pricing, how long can Western truck makers keep charging 2x diesel?

Diesel trucks aren’t the only thing batteries are displacing. At home, pairing solar with an EV or a home battery can cut your energy bills dramatically. #4391. After 15 years, The Sims' best spin-off finally gets its due follow-up in The Sims 4: Royalty & Legacy

The Sims Medieval had a short but powerful run back in 2011, and now many of its best features are finally coming to the main franchise.

The Sims 4 developers recently promised an exciting year for the game, and the franchise as a whole, and we just got an early look at one of those first events. After some light teasing, the developer unveiled Royalty & Legacy, the game’s next expansion.

Royalty & Legacy’s first trailer debuted on Thursday, revealing a February 12 release date, and showing off the expansion for the first time.

There’s a lot going on in Royalty & Legacy, which is priced $40. For one, it introduces a new world, Ondarion, which is going to be the setting for your kingdom, as you join a race for the throne. The expansion introduces Dynasty and Nobility - two new systems you can use to create your own world of royal shenanigans.

Ondarion is made up of three neighborhoods (regions). Each region has a unique theme and culture, and they’re each ruled by a Dynasty. Dambele is a place that prioritises art and community. Verdemar is a chaotic world of outlaws and nobles. Finally, Bellacorde is an extravagant region known for opulence and romance.

Speaking of building places, Royalty & Legacy also adds a new Lot type, The Backroom Lot. It serves two functions that change with the time of day. For instance, it can be a library or gym in the morning, and shift into a night club at night. Dambele has its own library-turned-rave, for instance.

At the heart of Ondarion are all the possible fantasy lives and stories you can live. The Sims calls them Powershifts, and they include some well-known Arthurian fantasies and other, more silly ones.

Swordsmanship is the new 10-level skill arriving with the expansion, which further plays into those fantasies by letting your Sims duel. There are even Swordsmanship Tournaments you can watch take place across every neighborhood in Ondarion.

Then there are Secret Passageways, which let you speed up moving across the new regions. They essentially let your Sims teleport between designated passageways, either on their own lots, or other lots in the world. Some of these are hidden for you to find, while others you can create.

In terms of new careers, there’s the Noble Career, where your Sim can rise through several Noble Rankings by doing basically what nobles had to do in the middle ages to earn favour.

The aforementioned Dynasty System is how you can join any of Ondarion’s existing families, or start your own. You actually have a lot of say in what goes on, including the usual business of appointing heirs.

Of course, no royal roleplay would be complete without scandals, which is where the Scandals System comes in. Through it, you can create stories to discredit others, or even topple an entire dynasty.

In November, you may recall The Sims 4 introducing new free items inspired by West African culture. In creating that content, EA worked with a group of Simmers who have direct ties to West African countries.

The group’s guidance was once again utilised to build the Dambele neighborhood in this expansion, and some of the lots around the world of Ondarion were even created by members of the group.

While you wait for Royalty & Legacy to actually arrive, there’s more in The Sims 4 you can jump in right now. The game recently kicked off a collaboration with fashion brand Coach that brought several free items to Create a Sim, and Build Buy. That arrived alongside a free update, which already makes for a busy start of the year for The Sims 4.

New Toyota RAV4 Has A Comfort Issue Some Owners Can't Ignore

The 2026 RAV4 is a welcome improvement, but one interior design flaw is frustrating some owners.

The latest, sixth-generation Toyota RAV4—introduced for the 2026 model year—is better than its predecessor in all the ways that count. Not only is it more efficient, but the RAV4’s performance, driving dynamics, and infotainment tech have all been praised. However, one interior design flaw has left several owners disgruntled. Described as a “huge design flaw” by one Reddit user, the issue relates to the especially wide center console, which eats into the amount of legroom. The problem affects certain owners much more than others, which seems to come down to height and/or one’s driving position. Is this a flaw Toyota should look into fixing, possibly with the RAV4’s first facelift? Let’s take a closer look.

In numerous threads on Reddit and other social media forums, owners of the RAV4 have criticized the design of the center console, which is particularly wide at the point where the driver’s right knee makes contact with it. An area of the console below the drive mode selector—and exactly where the USB-C ports are situated—digs into the knees of some drivers. To make matters worse, this area of the RAV4’s cabin features harder, scratchier plastics, further compounding the issue.

“Does anyone else find that the center console takes up too much space and pushes against your right leg/knee?” asked one user on Reddit. “I am 6’1” and the little outward curve of it makes my knee uncomfortable. There doesn’t seem to be any seat position that fixes this. Just picked it up from the dealership so I’m kinda bummed.”

Another Reddit user described the center console as “unnecessarily huge” and had a similar comfort complaint. Many RAV4 owners have now taken to installing makeshift pads or mini cushions, as can be seen in the video above.

While this may seem minor when compared to an engine failure (Tundra owners will know what we’re talking about), a comfort annoyance can significantly tarnish the driving experience, especially for drivers who spend many hours on the road.

At the same time, many drivers said the fat console doesn’t bother them or that adjusting their driving position was enough to alleviate the issue. In our various drives of the new RAV4, the wide center console was not a major issue, but that could be down to the seating position of our test drivers.

I Drove The 2026 Toyota RAV4 Woodland, Here’s My First Drive Review

Discover how the 2026 Toyota RAV4 Woodland blends rugged off-road capability with everyday comfort in our first drive review.

Leg space aside, the RAV4’s upgraded interior is generally better than the old one’s. The same console that takes up more leg space than some drivers prefer is otherwise very practical, with large cupholders and a reversible arm rest/storage bin. Easily accessible physical controls, phone charging trays, and USB-C charging ports are all integrated into this area. These features are useful, but it’s a lot to cram into a relatively compact space, which is likely why Toyota had to widen the center console.

The new infotainment interface is a major improvement. We found the system reassuringly glitch-free in our first drive of the RAV4, while the 10.5-inch (standard) or 12.9-inch (optional) touchscreens are easy to get to grips with. There’s enough space for adults at the back, too. If there is something we’d change, would like to see some brighter interior color schemes being offered on certain trims. The cabin can look a little drab when finished in black.

Toyota RAV4 Generations Overview: Evolution Of The Crossover Pioneer

Here’s how the RAV4 has changed across six generations.

A quick drive around the block is often not enough to accurately determine if a new car will suit your needs. As with any new car, we recommend that customers interested in a RAV4 spend sufficient time on the road in their preferred driving position to check if comfort levels are adequate. Still, we found enough complaints about this issue for Toyota to consider a light redesign of the RAV4’s console. At the very least, installing two soft knee pads on each side of the console could be a straightforward fix, and it would prevent buyers from having to find a makeshift solution.

#4388. Lexus is taking a page from China for its next electric SUV launching in 2027

Toyota’s luxury brand Lexus is launching a new electric SUV in 2027, its first vehicle built in China in over two decades.

It’s official. Toyota is breaking from tradition, planning to develop and produce the new vehicle in China rather than its home market of Japan.

Lexus confirmed the new vehicle will be made at its new manufacturing plant in Jinshan, Shanghai, and will go on sale in 2027.

As the first Lexus factory built from scratch overseas, the company said the new plant will bring together its global manufacturing capabilities.

Toyota broke ground on the facility in June 2025, saying the new facility will unlock “Lexus speed” as it aims to keep pace with domestic brands like BYD. Construction was expected to be completed this past August, with the first vehicle scheduled to roll off the assembly line in the fall of 2027.

The first Lexus model will be an electric SUV, produced using advanced manufacturing methods such as gigacasting to reduce costs and speed up output.

The facility will be a cornerstone of Toyota’s comeback plans in China, where it’s struggled to compete with local brands.

Production capacity will be around 1,000 units per month in 2027 as Toyota ramps up to “tens of thousands” in 2028.

Toyota’s sales plunged nearly 20% in China last month, marking its eighth consecutive month with lower sales than the year prior. The market in China “remained weak due in part to rising gasoline prices, while the market for gasoline vehicles and hybrid vehicles was particularly affected,” Toyota said.

In the first nine months of 2026, Toyota sold just over 1.05 million vehicles in China, 18.9% fewer than in the same period last year.

Lexus’ new Shanghai facility is wholly owned by Toyota, enabling it to produce vehicles in China through its joint ventures.

The new electric SUV will go on sale in China in 2027. Specific details, including battery, range, and prices, have yet to be announced.

As part of its “with China, for China, strategy, Lexus said it will “continue to use China as a source of innovation,” adding it will “deepen localization efforts” to bring classic models to the market that meet local needs.

Toyota joins the growing list of major OEMs that are already tapping, or plan to tap, China for its next-generation electric vehicles.

While in other global markets, Toyota is sticking to its “multi-pathway” strategy, which includes all powertrains from electric to ICE; in China, it’s being forced to adapt.

China is Toyota’s third-largest market, following the US and Japan. To stay competitive and turn things around in China, Toyota will rely more on local partners and suppliers.

Developing the new Lexus electric SUV in China first rather than Japan is significant given Toyota’s traditional ways.

Typically, it takes Toyota about four to five years to fully develop a new vehicle. In China, automakers are now building them in as little as two years.

Toyota, like many automakers at this point, is turning to China for new tech, batteries, production methods, and other EV components to keep pace.

#4387. The Karma Eximius 1 Is a One-Off Hybrid Packing a 6.2-Liter V-8

The track-ready sedan can zip to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and wears aggressive aerodynamics and carbon-fiber bodywork.

Personalization is the latest trend to sweep the automotive world, with nearly every high-end automaker launching a specific division that caters to the needs of its wealthiest customers. Porsche has Sonderwunsch, Bugatti has Sur Mesure, and Rolls-Royce has its Coachbuild program. Now Karma Automotive, a small American brand known for slinky plug-in hybrid sedans, is launching its own program called Eximius, and has revealed its first one-off, the Eximius 1, at the Concours at Wynn in Las Vegas.

Karma Automotive, if you aren’t familiar, was birthed from the ashes of Fisker Automotive, and has sold an evolution of the Fisker Karma, known as the Revero and GS-6, on and off for most of the past decade. The Revero is a series hybrid, with a turbocharged three-cylinder serving as a generator to charge a battery that feeds electricity to a pair of rear-mounted electric motors. Although the Revero is being replaced by the new Gyesera, which further hones the same design and powertrain philosophy, this year, Karma is making sure the Revero goes out with a bang with this new one-off.

See all results for used Karma for sale near 95125

The Eximius 1 takes the Revero platform and turns it up to eleven. This special one-off trades the three-cylinder for a far more compelling engine. Under the hood lies a 6.2-liter V-8, and the plug-in series hybrid powertrain produces a total of 1195 horsepower, which is well over 600 hp more than you get in the Revero. Karma claims the Eximius 1 can rocket to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and can hit a top speed of 200 mph. Given the Eximius 1’s more extreme performance, Karma has fitted it with carbon-ceramic, two-piece slotted brake rotors and Öhlins semi-active dampers.

The Eximius 1 is nearly two inches wider than a standard Revero, and carbon-fiber is used extensively throughout the car. Look closely at the bodywork, and you’ll be able to spot exposed carbon-fiber on the front fenders, with the blue paint fading in gradually over the carbon weave on the front doors, a truly unique finish. The Eximius 1 rides on 21-inch magnesium center-lock wheels.

Designed for driving on the track, the Eximius 1 sports a fittingly dramatic aerodynamic package. Up front, there’s a carbon front splitter, sandwiched by gaping air intakes that integrate an LED line, which, when viewed with the LED element in the headlights, creates an arrow shape pointing toward the center of the car. Two thin nostrils sit next to the headlights, giving the car a sinister sneer.

See all results for used Karma for sale near 95125

Vents have been carved into the front fenders to release air pressure from the wheel wells, and a large panel emblazoned with the number 5 incorporates a vent to extract hot air from the brakes. Below, a billet aluminum exhaust tip hints at the Eximius 1’s performance capabilities. An additional fin sits proud of the bodywork near the rear doors, and the rear end features a massive diffuser and a towering wing.

Inside, Karma has fitted blue-tinted carbon-fiber to the seats, steering wheel, center console, doors, and dashboard. The Recaro bucket seats are padded in blue Alcantara and blue leather on the bottom and Alcantara in a hue called Moondust up top. The accelerator, brake pedal, and dead pedal have been crafted from billet machined aluminum, and Karma simplified the center console to only include the necessary controls, including a red emergency kill switch.

The Eximius program will allow Karma’s customers to request modifications to the body, powertrain, and other performance components of the vehicle. Karma says it will create a maximum of nine bespoke vehicles based on each series production model that it launches. The Eximius 1 is the first, and it will be delivered to its owner in 2027.

#4386. BYD sold more EVs last month than the US did all quarter, topping 300,000

BYD sold over 300,000 electric vehicles in October, a new record and more than the US managed in the entire third quarter.

The world’s leading EV maker is showing no signs of slowing down. BYD sold 490,168 new energy vehicles (NEVs) in October, up 11% from the prior year and the company’s highest monthly total in 2026.

BYD’s battery electric vehicles drove the growth, with a record 305,743 units sold, up 37% year over year and marking the first time its EV sales have crossed the 300,000 mark.

To put that into perspective, just over 262,500 EVs were sold in the US in the entire third quarter combined, according to Kelley Blue Book estimates.

October marked BYD’s sixth straight month of higher sales growth and its third straight month of higher EV sales. Through October, BYD sold 1,953,700 electric vehicles, up 6% from the same period last year.

BYD’s all-electric vehicles (EVs) accounted for about 63% of total sales last month. Plug-in hybrid vehicles, meanwhile, fell 17% in October to 177,382 units. Through October, BYD’s PHEV sales fell 11% to 1,625,969 units.

According to BYD’s filing, the company exported 170,194 vehicles in October as it expands overseas to drive growth in markets like Europe, Southeast Asia, and Central and South America.

Through October, BYD exported over 1.5 million electric and plug-in hybrid vehicles, nearly double compared to last year.

By the end of 2026, BYD expects overseas shipments to reach about 2 million vehicles. In 2027, that number is expected to rise to more than 2.5 million vehicles.

There’s a lot of debate and heated discussions when it comes to AI. One one hand, it has been an effective assistant when used right, cutting down time when it comes to delegation and distribution of tasks. It has the ability to make more menial tasks that little bit less tedious, and can speed up workflow. Again, this is if the technology is used properly.

But with any new technology, it can also be used with malicious and criminal intent. The auto industry isn’t spared from that, and fraudsters can explore new possibilities to continue their activities with it.

In a report by Car Dealership Guy, organized networks are turning to auto financing fraud by exploiting gaps in security in digital automotive retail operations. Granted, it’s not a new thing, but AI has made it easier for criminal elements to do such schemes.

Per the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB), more synthetic identities are being flagged, and there’s now a higher incidence of credit washing and false theft claims. Other schemes include the submission of inflated or AI-fabricated pay stubs, and automated bot attacks on dealers and retailers. Dealers have reported a 77% increase in fraudulent activity over the past two years, while 24% of default cases have some links to fraud. As for credit washing, it skyrocketed to 228% from early 2024 to mid-2025.

The NICB says it estimates that $10.4 billion has been lost through these fraudulent lending schemes, and adds that number will be even higher this year. The agency also notes that nearly 70% of its vehicle finance fraud cases inflated or synthetic identities. It’s been estimated that each case costs aggrieved parties between $22,000 and $50,000. There have also been more elaborate schemes, with one such case involving an AI-generated cloned dealership scamming a buyer out of $77,300.

Financial fraud, as a whole, lowers economic productivity as it siphons cash flow from legitimate businesses to unsavory enterpises instead. It also erodes trust in an industry, and forces industries to put up more more rules to weed out criminal elements. But, in doing so, the cost of putting up more safeguards is passed on to the consumer via operational and administrative costs.

For dealers, this may lead them asking for even more requirements for the sake of identity verification, among other things. For consumers trying to fight fairly in life, it’s going through more hoops just to be able to buy a car. In its press release, the NICB “advocates for the modernization of state and federal statutory frameworks to close gaps exploited by synthetic identity rings,” with NICB COO Timothy R. Slater saying “Vehicle finance fraud has evolved from isolated credit misrepresentations into an organized, digital criminal industry that touches dealerships, lenders and insurers. Stopping these networks requires shifting away from reactive, siloed defenses toward standardized and synchronized cross-industry reporting.”

Mercedes-Benz is doubling down on the market that is hurting it most. According to Reuters, CEO Ola Källenius calls China an “indispensable market and innovation hub.

Third-quarter Mercedes-Benz Cars sales fell 8 percent to 407,232, with China down 31 percent to 86,800, according to BigGo. Elsewhere, Europe was up 5 percent, Germany was up 13 percent, and the US was up 6 percent, with record battery-electric sales up 61 percent. Adjusted return on sales for cars dropped to 2.5 percent from 4.8 percent, and Mercedes cut its full-year guidance to 2-3 percent from 3-5 percent; its CFO called the fourth quarter “a break-even quarter.”

Källenius said further German investment depends on productivity and costs, noting US labor costs run at roughly 80 percent of German levels.

#4380. How to Choose the Best Car Battery

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

Here's what you need to know to choose the right battery for your vehicle.

We've all experienced the stomach-churning trauma of a dead car battery. You need to be somewhere and you're running late. You jump in, twist the key or push the start button, and . . . nothing! Or maybe just a sickening click-click. Suddenly you need a jump-start or, worse, a tow. And probably a new battery, too. But which one?

So many brands, types, prices, and places to buy them. Which to choose and why? You don't need to be an expert to make an informed, cost-efficient purchase. Here are some brands we trust, but always check your owner’s manual for details and recommendations.

Check your owner's manual for your original battery's size, specifications, and ratings. You can also find which one you need from guides in the auto-parts store or online.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97229

Replacing a battery yourself is an option; it's not particularly difficult. Some shops offer free installation—but only if the battery is purchased from them.

If you're buying one of the batteries above online and installing it yourself, be sure to check your owner's manual for critical information before purchasing your new battery. Modern cars have specific requirements on their electrical systems, and the wrong power source could leave you stranded.

Most batteries are located up front, under the hood, where they're easy to access and replace with a couple of wrenches. But some are buried in the trunk or elsewhere—not so easy to find, let alone remove and replace.

Just remember, the negative terminal is always the first thing you disconnect and the last thing you reconnect.

Regardless of whether you're doing it in your driveway or letting a shop install, it's a good idea to first make sure you're buying the correct physical size. A number of sizes fit today's wide variety of vehicles.

For instance, size 24/24F (top terminal) batteries fit many Honda, Acura, Toyota, Lexus, Nissan, and Infiniti vehicles, while size 35 (top terminal) units fit many other Japanese vehicles, including recent Toyotas, Nissans, Hondas, and Subarus.

Size 48H6 (top terminal) batteries fit many European and American vehicles. Again, you can find which size you need in your owner's manual, in the replacement guides at the retail store, or online.

Almost all cars come with a 12-volt sealed lead-acid (SLA) battery of some variety (a few high-performance cars are equipped with lithium-ion batteries). These SLA batteries use the same chemistry as the ones your dad had to periodically top off with water, but today they are sealed—hence the name—and maintenance-free.

See all results for used cars for sale near 97229

Absorbent glass mat (AGM) batteries have quickly become the norm for most modern cars. They use similar chemistry as SLAs but are more durable and are claimed to stand up to more charge cycles.

Gel-cell batteries are best for deep discharging but may have problems in extreme hot or cold. Those old "wet cell" batteries from Dad's day are still available, though primarily for older models or penny pinchers. They are likely not offered in the right sizes and specs to support modern cars, however.

The next thing to check is the engine-cranking power of a vehicle battery, which is expressed in cranking amps (CA) and/or cold-cranking amps (CCA), a measure of how much electric current (in amperes) it can deliver for 30 seconds at 32 and zero degrees Fahrenheit. A bigger number is better, especially in cold weather, when batteries are at their weakest.

Another number to understand is the battery's reserve capacity, which is how long it can provide power with the engine off and headlights and/or accessories on or if the vehicle's charging system fails. One and a half hours is good. Two hours is better.

Also important is the warranty, which should be at least three years for full replacement (assuming no signs of neglect or abuse), plus, in some cases, a prorated refund for some time after that. Bear in mind, manufacturer warranties are often not supported when parts and accessories are purchased online from retailers like Amazon or Walmart.

Finally, be forewarned: Some brands, such as BMW, require the battery to be "coded" (digitally mated) to the car or it will not take a charge. Coding the battery requires BMW-specific OBD-II software that any reputable service shop or BMW dealer will have.

Expect to pay anywhere between $100 and $400 for a new battery, with lower-performing SLA types at the low end and stronger, longer-lasting AGMs near the top. If you're having it installed, the shop will dispose of your old battery.

If you're doing it yourself, take your old one to the retail outlet for recycling and to avoid a core charge—a mandatory deposit on your new battery that is refunded when you return the old one. Before you hand it over, place it side by side with the new battery to confirm the one you're buying is the same size. It's a final check to make sure your choice is the right one.

Oh, and if you're taking it home to install, get one with a traveling handle if possible—a car battery can weigh between 25 and 60 pounds.

#4379. Tomorrow's Battlefield 6 patch somehow makes jets more useless, improves armor bar visibility in Redsec

The first Battlefield 6 patch of the year is almost here, bringing a smattering of changes, including one that doesn't quite make sense.

Battlefield 6’s promised, season-extending update has been officially detailed. The patch, version 1.1.3.5, arrives tomorrow, January 20 right when Season 1 was supposed to end. Part of the update’s goal is to extend the current season, until Season 2 kicks off in the middle of February.

Update 1.1.3.5 does, of course, have a change log of its own that goes beyond just the season’s extension, but the changes fall somewhere between not very exciting, and a bit puzzling.

Patch 1.1.3.5 is, for all intents and purposes, a smaller update. When Battlefield Studios announced it earlier last week, the developer didn’t promise any major changes or fixes, so expectations never got out of hand.

The patch is mainly made up of bug fixes, but it does have three key areas of improvements to gameplay. There’s a big focus on melee combat, how responsive/unresponsive it is with the various melee tools, and how melee behaviour interacts with sprinting and other animations.

The end result should be faster attack speeds for the knife, and clearer wind-up animations for both the knife and the sledgehammer. The timing dictating when melee damage gets credited has also been made more consistent in different environments.

Interestingly, sprint is now only interrupted when the melee attack reaches its target. As it stands, sprinting is only interrupted after the full duration of the animation has been completed, which adds to the that perceived feeling of sluggishness.

The other major, and arguably most confusing is the nerf to jet cannons. The patch is going to make jets far less stronger against other air vehicles, requiring 40% more hits to destroy a target. This is puzzling because jets - and air vehicles in general - are already the least survivable in Battlefield 6.

And, considering how the rest of a jet's arsenal is either situational or nearly ineffective, the cannons were really the one guaranteed way of downing other air vehicles, so long as you manage to land your shots consistently. While the change is wellmeaning, the percentage will likely be reduced in future patches.

Finally, the update makes a few refinements to UI across the game, though mainly aimed at Redsec and modes where players wear armor. Armor bar visibility has been improved, and there’s a fix for the annoying bug that sometimes caused the armor bar to disappear every few seconds.

#4377. Tesla Powerwall 3 now boosts heat pumps to store cheap solar as heat

Tesla has launched Heat Pump Optimization, a feature that lets the Powerwall 3 and three-phase Powerwall 3P tell a compatible heat pump when to run harder so a home can bank cheap or surplus solar energy as hot water.

It’s live in Europe only. Tesla hasn’t said anything about bringing it to the US or Canada, and the hardware standard it relies on barely exists on this side of the Atlantic.

According to Tesla’s support page for the feature, the Powerwall watches electricity prices and solar production throughout the day and sends the heat pump one of two signals: run normally, or boost.

When it’s told to boost, the heat pump heats water beyond what the home needs right now, typically into a domestic hot water or buffer tank. That stored heat then carries the house through the expensive hours, when the heat pump can run less.

What triggers a boost depends on the Powerwall’s operating mode:

Tesla Energy summed it up on X last week: “Heat Pump Optimization allows your Powerwall to boost heating when there’s surplus solar or energy is inexpensive.”

There’s no cloud integration with heat pump brands here. It’s a wire.

The feature runs on SG-Ready (Smart Grid Ready), a label the German Heat Pump Association (BWP) introduced back in 2012 with 17 manufacturers. It uses two relay contacts on the heat pump to signal four operating states, from a utility block to a forced switch-on. Tesla only uses the “normal” and “boosted” recommendations.

Tesla’s requirements are pretty specific:

And there are limits. The signals are only recommendations, so the heat pump’s own thermostat settings can override them. Tesla also notes each signal has to be held for at least 10 minutes to comply with SG-Ready, and the feature drops back to normal during a power outage so the Powerwall can prioritize backup loads.

Oddly, there’s no on/off toggle in the Tesla app. Once it’s wired up, it’s on.

The math is what makes this interesting. A 300-liter hot water tank heated an extra 30°C holds about 10.5 kWh of thermal energy. With a heat pump running at a COP of 3, that takes only around 3.5 kWh of electricity to store.

So a tank most European heat pump homes already have can soak up a big chunk of midday solar without touching the lithium in the garage. That leaves the Powerwall’s 13.5 kWh free for the stuff that can’t be stored as heat.

The market is there too. Germany sold 299,000 heating heat pumps in 2025, up 55% year-over-year according to BWP, and they made up nearly half of all new heating systems sold in the country for the first time.

Tesla is also late to this. sonnen pushed a software update in 2023 that lets its sonnenBatterie run heat pumps off surplus solar, starting with NIBE units, and SG-Ready control has been a standard feature of German PV energy managers for years.

I'd love to have a hot water driven radiant heat system paired with solar and battery storage and a smart management system. Unfortunately, the US seems to lag behind on this, but my sense is that even in Europe the integration between all the components isn't yet as smooth as would be desired.

It’s the latest Europe-first move for Tesla Energy after it launched the Powerwall 3P with a native three-phase inverter earlier this year, aimed squarely at Germany, Austria, and Switzerland. The company announced its 1 millionth Powerwall last year, and software like this is how it squeezes more value out of that installed base.

This is a smart, cheap feature, and it’s exactly the kind of thing that makes a home battery more valuable without adding a single cell.

Heat is the biggest energy load in most homes in cold climates, and water is about the cheapest storage medium there is. Using a battery’s brain to time the heat pump around solar and tariffs makes a lot more sense than discharging lithium to run a compressor at 6 p.m.

Home batteries are changing the economics of residential energy, and pairing them with solar (and smart loads like heat pumps) is the best way to get the most out of them. McLaren’s first manual-transmission car in more than three decades is now out in public. The McLaren McL 6GT made its global public debut at the 2026 Concours at Wynn Las Vegas. The big news: it has a clutch pedal. The McL 6GT pairs a mid-mounted V8 with a six-speed manual transmission that drives the rear wheels. That makes it the first McLaren road car with a true manual since the McLaren F1 arrived in 1992. A production version is due in 2028.

The McL 6GT takes its name and its mission from the M6GT, the road car Bruce McLaren began developing in the late 1960s. The M6GT was based on the M6A Can-Am racer. It was meant to be the first true McLaren road car and possibly the basis for a Le Mans program. Bruce drove the prototype as his personal car, but the project ended when he died in 1970. McLaren Special Operations recently restored his original car using archive drawings, the original body molds and period photos.

The McL 6GT is built on a carbon-fiber monocoque with all-carbon bodywork. McLaren says the car is about the connection between driver and machine, not outright performance, and the hardware reflects that. It gets hydraulically assisted steering, knurled machined-aluminum controls and a gear lever tuned specifically for shift feel and throw.

The exterior borrows from the M6A: a low, wide body, a Kammback tail and a “Racing Loop” taillight motif inspired by the original M6GT. Bruce McLaren’s signature sits in the engine bay, his M6GT registration plate appears as a tone-on-tone graphic, and the “Speedy Kiwi” emblem shows up on the fuel cap and the gear knob.

Most of the segment has moved to dual-clutch transmissions and electrification, so the McL 6GT shows that a major supercar maker still sees a business case for a manual. For collectors, it’s a low-volume, heritage-driven McLaren with a 2028 delivery window. Watch for pricing and allocation details as production gets closer.

With a long-travel suspension and turbos from the R35 GT-R, this heavily modded mid-size truck is a hardcore desert runner.

In true SEMA fashion, Nissan’s aim for the Frontier Ronin concept was to create an “unstoppable off-road truck.” To that end, the automaker stretched the limits of the Frontier platform’s performance in terms of both the truck’s powertrain and off-road capabilities.

The Frontier’s 3.8-liter V-6 is still present under the hood of the Ronin, but Nissan also made a host of notable changes. For starters, the Ronin features forced induction in the form of the R35 Nissan GT-R’s twin-turbo setup, which is mounted in the rear.

The engine is fed air through a set of custom intakes and kept cool thanks to a custom front-mounted intercooler system. Unfortunately, Nissan hasn’t divulged exactly how much power the system generates, but it’s sure to be a good deal more than the Frontier’s stock 310 ponies.

More power is great, but it’s important to have somewhere to use it. Nissan reached into the parts bin for the larger Titan’s rear axle as well as its suspension for a bit of further modification.

The whole thing rides on a set of prototype NISMO Ascend beadlock wheels and a set of Yokohama Geolandar X-AT tires.

#4373. Cadillac’s most affordable EV just got a bit cheaper

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range, a massive 33″ infotainment screen, an NACS charge port, and now it’s a bit more affordable.

The Optiq first went on sale in 2025 as Cadillac’s entry-level electric SUV, starting at $54,390. For the 2026 model year, the Optiq arrived as GM’s first electric vehicle with a built-in NACS port and added a new rear-wheel-drive (RWD) powertrain.

Thanks to the new RWD option, the 2026 Optiq (see our review) was also slightly less expensive, with prices starting at $52,395.

While GM initially said the 2027 Cadillac Optiq would start at $52,695, prices on its website have been updated and are now slightly lower.

The base 2027 Cadillac Optiq Luxury RWD is now listed at $51,790, or $905 less than the initial price announced months ago. The Luxury AWD trim is also $905 cheaper, starting at $55,290.

Meanwhile, the Sport trim now starts at $52,395 for RWD and $55,895 for AWD, both $900 less than before.

The higher-spec Optiq Premium Luxury, Premium Sport, and V-Series trims remain at the price GM initially announced.

The 2027 Cadillac Optiq offers up to 317 miles of range in the RWD models and 303 miles with AWD. All models come with a standard 33″ Horizon Display infotainment screen, a 19-speaker AKG Studio Audio System, GM’s Super Cruise hands-free driver-assist technology, and a native NACS charge port.

Upgrading to AWD costs an extra $3,500. The Premium Luxury and Premium Sport add standard features including a Head-Up Display, ventilated and lumbar massaging front seats, and a rear cargo cover.

The high-performance 2027 Optiq-V starts at $69,295 and delivers a Cadillac-estimated 519 lb-ft of torque and 650 horsepower in Velocity MaX Mode,

How does the Cadillac Optiq stack up against the Tesla Model Y? The base Tesla Model Y RWD starts at $39,990 with up to 321 miles of range, while the AWD version costs $41,990 and gets up to 294 miles.

The Tesla Model Y Premium RWD starts at $45,990 with up to 355 miles of range, while the Premium AWD starts at $49,990 and has 327 miles of range.

The two are nearly the same size, but the Tesla Model Y offers slightly more rear legroom and cargo capacity than the Cadillac Optiq.

If you ever wondered where automotive YouTube sensation Doug DeMuro dreams up his daily content, the answer is appropriately unusual. Three stories below ground, entirely windowless, and accessible only via a dedicated, heavy-duty car elevator, the official Cars and Bids headquarters looks and functions exactly like a billionaire superhero’s secret automotive lair. This subterranean garage serves simultaneously as an active vehicle storage facility, an open-concept corporate office, and a fully equipped television production studio.

Because the massive concrete room lacks any interior walls or soundproofing, conducting daily corporate business here requires some incredibly creative workarounds. When DeMuro is actively filming vehicle reviews under the bright studio lights, employees are completely forbidden from taking meetings or having loud conversations due to the aggressive echo. As a result, when the staff needs to make a private phone call or join a Zoom meeting, they simply climb into a manual BMW X5 or whatever classic sports car happens to be parked nearby, essentially turning the inventory into highly expensive office cubicles.

The Petersen Automotive Museum YouTube channel featured Doug’s garage and the inventory parked beneath the streets of San Diego is exactly as quirky as you would expect from DeMuro. Rather than focusing exclusively on multi-million dollar exotics, the basement is filled with a fascinating, rotating cast of low-mileage oddities and future classics currently awaiting review and auction. On any given day, the floor space might feature a mint-condition Nissan Pathfinder with just 800 original miles, an ultra-rare Lotus 340R, or a pristine third-generation Acura TL.

The staggering inventory continues with a low-mileage Pontiac Firebird Ram Air, a V12 Aston Martin Vanquish, a front-wheel-drive Lotus Elan, a fifth-generation Dodge Viper SRT, and a 1960s Alfa Romeo TZ. Rounding out the diverse auction lineup is a Nissan Skyline R34, a turbo-diesel Toyota Land Cruiser 80 series, a right-hand-drive Ford Sierra Cosworth, and a 2009 Maserati GranTurismo uniquely converted to a gated six-speed manual.

While DeMuro famously drove his 2005 Ford GT across the country rather than preserving it like an 8-mile museum piece, his current personal fleet parked in the lair includes a beloved Lamborghini Countach and a worn 1999 Mercedes-Benz G500 Cabriolet. Employee Ryan Lopez’s custom “Zesty” drift car also shares the floor. Beyond the vehicles, the facility is thoroughly equipped to keep the Cars and Bids team operating around the clock, featuring a full kitchen routinely stocked with donuts, a laundry room, and a full bathroom.

When the team actually takes a break from reviewing rare Japanese imports and manual-swapped Maseratis, they retreat to a sprawling entertainment section. The hangout space includes a large putting green, comfortable couches, and an incredibly high-end racing simulator custom-built by Linus Tech Tips. The sim is even connected to a physical leaderboard, proving that even when they are off the clock, the crew never truly stops chasing lap times. Ultimately, this hidden subterranean bunker serves as the perfect headquarters for the rapidly growing auction platform, perfectly reflecting the passionate and quirky car culture DeMuro has championed for over a decade.

#4371. Hardee’s gets EV fast charging – with Carl’s Jr. locations to follow

EV drivers have a new reason to pull into Hardee’s. Energized EV has opened four fast-charging ports at a restaurant in Temple, Georgia, kicking off a planned rollout at Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. locations across the US.

There’s no site count or rollout schedule yet, but the first location is open with both NACS and CCS1 connectors.

The chargers are at 587 Carrollton Street in Temple. The site has two dual-port XCharge C7 DC fast chargers, each rated at 240 kW, for a total of four charging ports. Monta provides the chargers’ software. XCharge says the C7 adjusts power output between its two connectors, and both NACS and CCS1 connectors are on offer.

“Adding charging at our restaurants gives EV drivers a convenient place to stop, recharge, and enjoy a meal,” said Mike Darger, vice president of facilities and maintenance at CKE Restaurants. “We look forward to building on this first opening as more locations come online across the country.”

Energized EV says more Hardee’s and Carl’s Jr. sites are planned across the US, with president and CEO Devin Grandis calling Temple “the beginning of a much larger expansion.”

Energy & Environmental Design Services LLC (E&EDS) is the program’s exclusive installer. Its services include charging infrastructure design, installation, and maintenance, as well as electrical contracting.

Energized EV’s approach is to install chargers where drivers already stop, whether they’re running errands or taking a longer road trip. But we’ll need the next locations and opening dates to see how useful this restaurant charging network will become. The announcement doesn’t list charging prices for Temple.

Ford and Chevrolet may be the most recognized brands in the American racing scene, but Ferrari once considered joining the fray. In the 1980s, company founder Enzo Ferrari was frustrated with Formula 1 politics and proposed regulation changes, and threatened to leave the sport. He commissioned the Ferrari 637 in 1986 for a potential entry into the CART Indy Car World Series and the Indy 500, but it never entered a race.

There was another vehicle that came out of that unusual chapter of the Prancing Horse brand’s history, which led CART entrants on the track. Well, the vehicle in question is a one-off Ferrari Mondial designed to serve as a pace car. A recent video uploaded by AVANTS on YouTube brought the pace car, now part of The Caretakers Collection, back into the spotlight, sharing some interesting bits about an American venture that never fully materialized.

The Ferrari Mondial pace car was part of the PPG Pace Car program, which fielded different vehicles at CART events, including a 1983 Dodge Daytona Turbo Z and a 1992 Subaru SVX. While the Mondial wasn’t as celebrated as Ferrari models like the Testarossa, this particular pace car has some interesting provenance.

For one, the Ferrari pace car reportedly cost $1 million to build in 1987, which, adjusted to today’s money, is around $3 million. Designed by Italian firm I.DE.A Institute, the pace car came with an extended wheelbase, redesigned front and rear bodywork, and, of course, integrated warning lights. It also featured a brake-cooling system that sprayed water through nozzles. The cabin, meanwhile, featured a custom dashboard and steering wheel, along with Kevlar and suede accents.

Powering the PPG project was an experimental 3.4-liter V8 producing a reported 300 horsepower. Forza Magazine said that the engine was being developed for the upcoming Ferrari 348. So, aside from just leading the field, the pace car also served as an early showcase for the automaker’s upcoming powertrain technology.

This Ferrari Mondial pace car isn’t for sale. But it offers a glimpse into a lesser-known era of the Italian marque’s history, especially considering the brand is better known for its strong presence in F1.

Today, the IndyCar Series uses different pace cars depending on the event, with the 2026 Indy 500 paced by the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1X. In F1, the duties of the pace car, better known as the safety car, are handled by the Mercedes-AMG GT 63 PRO 4MATIC+.
